#9682. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9680. Resize an Image in the Browser: Three Numbers That Move Together

Most resize tools give you a slider or a handful of presets. That is fine until you need an exact pixel size for a form, a sprite sheet or a CMS that rejects anything else - at which point you end up guessing and checking the result by hand.

The Image Studio's Resize tab in OnePassApps takes the opposite approach: it shows you the width, the height and the scale of your image as live numbers, tells you which of them are locked, and hands you the resized file so you can check it yourself.

Full disclosure: I work on OnePassApps. This is the Resize tab in the Image Studio, checked in the live tab while writing this - every number below came out of a run I made, not out of the marketing copy.

The Image Studio carries seven tool tabs on one page: Convert, Compress, Resize, Crop, Remove background, Remove metadata, Images to PDF. The page line above them reads "Convert, compress, resize, crop and clean images in your browser. Nothing leaves this tab."

The Resize tab is laid out as three numbered steps.

01 Source - "Add an image to start. Your original stays untouched." The picker accepts JPEG, PNG or WebP · up to 25 MiB and 25 megapixels, and the page repeats "Processing stays in this browser."

02 Dimensions - "Width, height and scale appear here once an image is open. They start at its real size." Three number fields - Width (px), Height (px) and Scale (%) - then two checkboxes, Lock aspect and Prevent upscaling, a Format row of PNG, JPEG and WebP, a Quality control, and the line "Resampled in this browser, up to 25 megapixels."

03 Result - "The new copy's size and format appear here."

The action button is Resize image, and after a run it becomes "Resize again". The panel also carries a "Fit" / "100%" preview zoom and a Result / Original toggle so you can compare the two side by side.

Open a 400 × 300 image and the fields read 400, 300 and 100. Type 100 into the width and the height does not stay at 300 - it becomes 75, and the scale drops to 25. That is the Lock aspect checkbox doing its job: it is on by default, and it keeps the ratio of your image while you resize it.

Set the scale instead and the other two follow. Scale 50 on the same 400 × 300 image gave 200 × 150 automatically.

So with the lock on, you type one number and the panel does the arithmetic. The fields are not three separate settings; they are three views of the same decision.

The limits are visible in the markup rather than buried: width and height run from 1 to 12000, the scale field from 1 to 400, and the quality control from 10 to 100, starting at 86.

Prevent upscaling is also on by default, and it is the one that surprises people. With it on, typing a width larger than the source is refused: on the 400 × 300 image, entering 800 left the field reading 400, with the height back at 300 and the scale back at 100.

Turn it off and the same 800 is accepted. The width field became 800, the height followed to 600, and the scale showed 200.

That is a deliberate guard rather than a limit on the format. Enlarging a 400 × 300 image to 800 × 600 invents 240,000 pixels that were never in the file - they are filled in by interpolation, so you get a bigger file with less real detail in it. The checkbox is there so that "make it bigger" is something you ask for on purpose.

Here is the run, in full, on a 400 × 300 PNG I generated myself (four flat colour quadrants with a black marker square in the top-left corner).

Run 1 - downscale to 100 px wide. Width 100, lock aspect on, default JPEG. The panel reported:

The exported file was a real JPEG - 1,378 bytes with a JFIF header. Reading its pixels back, the top-left pixel was black (0,0,0,255), the top-right green (0,255,0,255), the bottom-left blue (0,0,255,255) and the bottom-right white (255,255,255,255): the same four quadrants, resampled into the smaller frame, in the same places.

Run 2 - upscale to 800 px wide. Prevent upscaling off, width 800. The panel reported "Dimensions 400 × 300 → 800 × 600", "After 6.9KiB JPEG" and "JPEG · 800 × 600 · 6.9 KiB · 290% larger". The exported file was 7,064 bytes of JPEG, and the four corner pixels still read black, green, blue and white.

Run 3 - PNG output at 120 px wide. Format PNG, width 120, height followed to 90, scale 30. The panel reported "After 618B PNG", "Dimensions 400 × 300 → 120 × 90", "PNG · 120 × 90 · 618 B · 66% smaller". The exported file's IHDR header read 120 × 90, and its corner pixels read black, green, blue and white again.

The Format row defaults to JPEG, so the first resize I made came out as "probe-resize.jpg" even though the source was a PNG.

Read the size line before you take it. Upscaling that flat-colour PNG to 800 × 600 produced "6.9 KiB · 290% larger" - the file got three and a half times the size of the original, because JPEG re-encodes what PNG had stored losslessly and the result is still only 400 × 300 of real pixels. The panel is not hiding it: it shows the before and after sizes, the percentage, and a Result / Original toggle so you can compare the two.

Pick PNG when you want a lossless result. The same downscale to 120 × 90 came out at 618 bytes, against 1.8 KiB for the source - 66% smaller, and every pixel in it still exactly matches the colour it came from.

The result panel gives you the file name, the format, the pixel dimensions, the size change, the time it took ("Resized in 0.2 s"), and a Download button. The closing line is the honest one: "Finished. Download a new copy; the original stays unchanged." Your source file is never overwritten, and you keep both copies side by side.

The usual reason to resize something is that it goes somewhere you do not control - an upload box that wants exactly 800 × 600, a form with a size limit, an avatar field that wants a square. Those are exactly the files you would rather not hand to a stranger's server, and this tab never sends them: the page says "Nothing leaves this tab." and "Processing stays in this browser.", and the only thing that leaves the browser is the file you download yourself.

#9679. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9678. Your AI Agent's Memory Needs Two Clocks

Consumer agents run for years with the same user. A companion, a coach, or a journaling app collects thousands of small facts, most of which are only true for a while or evolve over time. Things like a race next Sunday, a trial ending in January, a trip last week, etc. With time, the memories stay in the pool even after the event time has passed.

Most setups store what the user said and when the system stored it, and nothing about when it actually happened. And the agent has no way to tell what is still true at retrieval time. For continuity, we will use one running example in this article - a fitness coach app called Stride, with a user named Sam.

Event time is when the thing happened: Sam ran the race on Sunday. Write time is when your app got to know about it: during a user’s chat session or during a later data import. Tracking these two independent timelines, when the event happened and when the system learned about it, is bitemporal reasoning, and relational databases have done it for decades. Most memory setups keep only write time, and that holds until the two timelines disagree. They disagree often, and we’ll discuss the list of possible cases here.

Stride has run for two years and wants to import old chats. Sam wrote "I ran my first 10K last weekend" in June 2025. Store it today, and the system reads "last weekend" against today, so the memory becomes "Sam ran a 10K this week," wrong by a year and stuck that way since the import loses the original date. Pass the original conversation time on every write and resolve the phrase against it.

The stored memory now reads "User ran a 10K on the weekend of 2025-06-14 to 2025-06-15," its created date reads June 2025, and a date filter for June 2025 finds it.

Sam says "I started the new knee meds yesterday." Resolve the phrase at write time, because only then do you know the actual conversation date, and store the date instead of the word. You also need a precision scale: "yesterday" is a day, "last month" is a month, and you should not invent an exact day from a vague phrase. Pass the exact instant the message was sent so time zones work out. "This morning" sent at 5 AM in Singapore is still the previous day in UTC.

Sam is vegetarian, then starts eating fish. Sam lives in Lisbon, then moves to Berlin. Both were true at different times, and a coach app that mixes them suggests tofu for lunch recommendations in a city Sam doesn’t live in anymore. Do not delete the old fact. It needs to be retained and linked to the new fact to create a chain of events. A user may ask need the current value or the history depending on different cases:

"Training for the Berlin half on Nov 15" should stop affecting responses after Nov 15. "Dry January" ends Jan 31. Certain memories need an expiration setting at the time of writing, and the expiration should hide a memory rather than delete it, because the record still matters for history. The memory needs to stay visible through the date and drop out of search results the day after, with a way to show expired ones on request.

Before each reply, the coach app asks "what did Sam struggle with last week?" or "my knee injury’s progress from July to September." Two tools do different jobs:

Pass "now" into each read instead of letting the system decide the time autonomously. A nightly job at 02:00 UTC is morning in Singapore and the previous evening in San Francisco. An eval asking "what would the app have known on 2026-03-21?" should stay fixed as the day changes. A reference date fixes this.

After 18 months, 2025 knee injury memories continue to match for the keyword "knee." Memory age alone is not a strong enough signal; how often a memory still gets retrieved is a stronger one. Memories need to be retrieved based on usage-based reranking and not directly filtered, so a two-year-old allergy stays reachable while a healed injury drifts down, and comes back up only if Sam specifically mentions the knee again.

Sam says "I told you about my injury and you still pushed me to run hills." You need a way to reliably investigate what the app knew on a given day. Pull every memory written up to that date without any filters, and check whether the injury's creation date precedes the hill session.

For a single memory, its change history should return each write and update with the old text, the new text, and when it changed.

If you build or buy a memory layer for long-running consumer agents, these are the knobs it needs:

event-time, duration, and precision parameters on write

linking chain of events, with a current-only filter

an expiry field, plus a way to show expired

created-at filters with required logic operations

a created-at filter with per-memory history

The idea is simple: track both event time and write time for every memory with the above parameters and filters, and your app’s memory setup should be able to take care of almost all time-related scenarios.

Multi-tenant agent memory isolation is a filtering problem, not a ranking problem

#9676. Music Through Your Cheekbones: How Bone-Conduction Headphones Work and Why They Sound Different

Reetain Raina, a Technical Writer specializing in wearable technology, AI, smart glasses and future consumer tech.

Reetain Raina, a Technical Writer specializing in wearable technology, AI, smart glasses and future consumer tech.

Reetain Raina, a Technical Writer specializing in wearable technology, AI, smart glasses and future consumer tech.

Most headphones function in a very simple manner: sound waves created by the headphones propagate through the air into the ear canal and into the inner ear. However, there are some headphones that have a non-traditional approach to producing sound for listening to music. These headphones can deliver sounds through vibrations to the head bones and tissues, thus enabling users to listen to music without inserting earbuds into the ear canals or using bulky headphones that cover them completely.

Such headphones are called bone-conduction headphones, as they produce vibrations in addition to the conventional sounds created by speakers.

It may appear strange, but the science behind this process is fairly simple. In fact, there is always some kind of bone conduction when a person speaks and hears his own voice. Vibrations generated by the act of speaking pass not only through the air but through the body, which explains why the voice that is recorded differs from the voice we hear when speaking.

In addition, transmission of sounds via the head affects how music is being played. In order to explain why this happens, it is necessary to learn more about how these headphones function and how sound vibration turns into music.

Before diving into the mechanics of bone conduction, it helps to establish exactly how normal headphones work. Understanding this baseline makes the technical jump to bone conduction much easier to follow.

Headphones are designed based on the principle of air conduction and transmit sound into the inner ear in the following way. First, sound waves are produced from the headphones as a result of a diaphragm's rapid vibration. These waves move through the air inside the ear canal and eventually encounter the eardrum that starts vibrating.

Then, three small bones in the middle ear, called malleus, incus and stapes, amplify the vibrations and pass them on to the cochlea. It is an incredibly small organ located in the inner ear, which has the shape of a snail and contains fluid. Moreover, it consists of a basilar membrane, which separates the liquid inside the cochlea. As the waves move through the liquid, the sensory hair cells convert mechanical energy to the electrical one. Finally, the signals reach the brain through the auditory nerve, which interprets them as sound. However, the eardrum is not the only place for vibrations to get to the cochlea.

Whereas miniature speakers have been traditionally used, modern consumer bone-conduction headphones make use of transducers that are electromechanical. This is because the main function of these transducers is to convert electrical audio signals to mechanical vibration. This is different from normal headphones since the transducer does not go inside or on the ears. They usually come into contact with the skin around the ear region.

Hearing using a bone conduction device is quite distinct from the one used by earbuds. Once the audio signal sent from the computer to the headphones has been received, it gets converted into mechanical waves through the transducer inside. The transducer moves in sync with the skin of your face and the body tissues beneath it.

This vibration travels through the biological parts of your head, without interacting with the outer and middle ear at all. Mechanical energy turns into motion in the cochlear region. From here, the entire process becomes just like any other form of hearing process, where the sensory hair cells detect the motion in the fluid and send signals to the brain through the auditory nerve.

It is easy to picture bone conduction as one simple process involving the skull, but the reality of it is actually quite complicated. The process of transmission of sounds through the head includes more than one pathway operating at once.

As described in the basic research on bone-conducted sounds and their physiology, there are a number of different ways that this is accomplished. Vibrations lead to movement of the fluid within the cochlea, called cochlear fluid inertia, which is one of the main factors that allow us to hear bone-conducted sounds. Also, the small bones of the middle ear react to the vibration of the skull (ossicle inertia). Moreover, the vibrations cause micro-movement of the walls of the cochlea. Surprisingly, vibrations of the skull also produce secondary sound pressure within the ear canal.

If you have ever tried a pair of bone-conduction headphones, you immediately notice that they do not reproduce sound in exactly the same way as conventional earbuds. The audio often feels different in texture and weight. This variance comes down to the transducers, the physical vibration pathways and how human tissue filters different frequencies.

Bass sounds that have lower frequencies are critical in the listening experience of music in modern times. In the case of regular earphones, changes in air pressure are used effectively in stimulating the eardrum. In the case of bone conduction headphones that people can buy, the sound waves have to fight their way to the cochlea through a combination of skin, cartilage and bone tissues.

Human tissue has a natural tendency to dampen certain mechanical frequencies, thus, the production of bass tones is noticeably less intense. The transducers have to vibrate more in order for bass tones to be produced, thus, there will be a noticeable buzzing and tickling effect on the cheekbones of the listener.

Since the transducers are placed totally outside of the ear canal and operate by making vibrations outside of the head, part of the acoustic energy is bound to leak out into the air. As a result, there will be sound leakage, which means that people who happen to be sitting close to you can overhear the low-quality music leaking from the earphones. Additionally, the open-ear technology allows all kinds of background noises to get into your ears automatically.

Designing consumer bone-conduction wearables requires engineers to navigate a highly specific set of physical limitations. Building a traditional speaker is mostly about moving ai, building a bone-conduction transducer is about effectively transferring mechanical energy into the human body.

The issue of positioning the transducer is significantly more complicated than just finding a place where it will be able to vibrate. The exact position of the transducer, the force of its pressure on the skin and the coupling with the underlying tissue will determine the efficiency of vibrations reaching the inner ear.

One particularly intriguing experiment conducted in 2023 on bone conduction hearing via bone conduction headsets revealed precisely this connection. It was found out that vibrating the area near the opening of the ear canal greatly increased bone conduction sensitivity by about 20 dB compared to the classical position of the transducer behind the ear (mastoid bone) with the highest sensitivity increase of up to 40 dB on certain frequencies.

Engineers always find themselves in the midst of a tug-of-war when it comes to trade-offs. The vibration can be enhanced in the transducer, which may result in improved bass and volume, however, very soon, it will result in skin fatigue for the user. A more tight headband provides better mechanical coupling and sound transmission, but it results in a headache due to the pressure exerted on the head.

The most defining visual characteristic of these headphones is that they leave the ear entirely unobstructed. By resting on the temporal bone or cheekbone, they do not physically block the ear canal in any way.

The open ear technology allows normal transfer of environmental sound through the air to your eardrum despite you listening to a podcast or music. It addresses the issue of situational awareness that is faced by a particular user segment. Bicyclists would be able to hear any coming traffic, office workers can listen to music and still be aware of their colleagues and even runners can have spatial awareness around them.

But most importantly, it needs to be realized that having an open ear feature does not mean that it automatically provides you with safety. Listening to loud playback using bone conduction technology may mentally distract the listeners and loud environmental sound would also be enough to mask the audio you are listening to. What's more, no consumer bone conduction headsets provide any kind of passive noise cancellation.

It is a mistake to view consumer bone-conduction technology as a direct upgrade or replacement for conventional headphones. Instead, both technologies solve fundamentally different listening problems.

They are perfect for those people who have trouble wearing regular ear buds because of discomfort or the tendency for them to fall out. They are great options for outdoor sportsmen, urban travelers and anyone else who wants to have their own music soundtrack while staying engaged with reality.

If you’re someone who requires high-fidelity sound quality, then the concept of bone conduction won’t work for you. Over-the-ear or in-the-ear headphones have a far more superior performance when it comes to deep bass, wide soundstage and an immersive experience. The one purpose for which bone conduction headphones can’t fulfill their purpose is to cancel the noise of an airplane or noisy café.

In addition to traditional methods of listening to music, the technology of bone conduction is opening new classes of wearable devices for consumers. This is because the bone-conduction system does not occlude the ear canal and it is increasingly becoming an integral part of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses and spatial computing visors.

While using AR glasses, you need your digital data to be laid over the real one. Bone conduction transducers integrated into the arm of smart glasses can provide you with directions, responses of your virtual assistant and even chime notifications without isolating you from your environment. In tactical, outdoors and sports communications, it allows team members to coordinate themselves through voice communication while remaining fully acoustically aware of their environment.

Ultimately, the emergence of bone conduction technology demonstrates an interesting biological phenomenon - the fact that sound doesn’t always have to pass through the ear canal to be audible. This kind of headphones shows how versatile the human auditory system can be in its ability to convert mechanical vibrations via different physical paths into our beloved music.

Although their distinctive transfer method restricts the capabilities of the headphones in terms of bass reproduction and noise isolation, it provides a truly unique combination of digital sound and physical perception. In case our brain can easily process the sound via vibrations transmitted through the skull, what other physical paths could be used by future wearables to change our digital experiences?

Reetain Raina, a Technical Writer specializing in wearable technology, AI, smart glasses and future consumer tech.

#9675. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9674. Ask AI providers, and where your key lives

JSLab feature notes: one docs page, explained. Today: AI providers and keys.

JSLab's Ask AI panel answers questions about the code in your tab and returns changes as a diff. It doesn't come with a model of its own: it uses your own key, or Ollama locally. This note is about that setup.

Everything lives in Settings → AI. Provider starts at None, which turns AI Chat off. The other choices:

Ollama is a separate, free program that runs models on your own Mac. Install and start it yourself, choose Ollama (Local), and you're done. No key.

Here's AI Chat in a real JSLab tab with Ollama as the provider: the provider shows as a chip at the top of the panel, and the question goes to the model on your own Mac.

Each provider has its own Model field. Leave it blank for the default that ships with this version of JSLab, or type the name you want. The field also lists the models the provider reports; for Ollama, that's the models you've installed. Refresh fetches the list again.

There's a Base URL per provider too. Blank means the standard endpoint above; set it to point at, say, an Ollama server on another machine.

The API Keys section of Settings → AI has a field for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Gemini. Paste a key, click Save, and the field shows A key is stored. Remove deletes it.

Each message carries JSLab's instructions, the current tab's code (up to 100 KB), the conversation so far, and your message. With Send Recent Output on (the default), the last run's output goes too, up to 20 KB. Turn it off to send only code and conversation. Nothing else from your Mac is sent, and with Ollama at its standard local address, none of it leaves your Mac.

JSLab launches Nov 15. The full page: https://js-lab.app/docs/ai-providers

#9673. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9672. Crafting Incident Response Plans that Fulfill ISO 27001 and SOC 2

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at blog.bitkoshtechnologies.com

In today's digital landscape, organizations must prioritize security and compliance to safeguard sensitive information. Both ISO 27001 and SOC 2 are critical frameworks that help organizations demonstrate their commitment to security, but aligning their requirements can be a challenge. One essential element of both frameworks is the Incident Response Plan (IRP). In this blog post, we will explore how to develop an incident response plan that meets the requirements of both ISO 27001 and SOC 2, ensuring compliance while enhancing security posture.

To effectively create a compliant incident response plan, it's crucial to understand the specific requirements of both ISO 27001 and SOC 2.

ISO 27001 is an international standard focused on information security management systems (ISMS). The standard requires organizations to:

To develop an effective incident response plan that fulfills both ISO 27001 and SOC 2 requirements, consider the following steps:

Conducting a gap assessment will help identify areas where your current incident response plan falls short of both frameworks. This involves reviewing existing policies and procedures, assessing risks, and identifying compliance gaps. Engage with stakeholders across the organization to gather diverse insights and data, which will create a well-rounded understanding of your current state.

Clearly define the roles and responsibilities of team members during an incident response. This ensures that everyone knows who to contact and what actions to take when an incident occurs. Both ISO 27001 and SOC 2 emphasize the importance of defined roles, which can help streamline communication and decision-making during a crisis.

Create detailed procedures that outline the steps to take when an incident is detected. This should include:

Effective communication is essential during an incident. Your incident response plan should include:

Regular training and awareness programs are vital to ensure that all staff members understand their role in the incident response process. Conduct simulations and tabletop exercises that reflect real scenarios to help staff practice their responses. This approach will help enhance the overall readiness of your organization for any potential incidents.

Both ISO 27001 and SOC 2 require organizations to regularly test their incident response plans. Schedule periodic reviews and drills to assess the effectiveness of your procedures. Use these tests to identify areas for improvement and update your plan accordingly. Integrating tools and frameworks for security testing can help ensure compliance and validate your incident response plan's effectiveness.

Documenting the incident response process is critical for compliance with both frameworks. Maintain records of incidents, responses, and reviews, which will provide valuable evidence during audits. After each incident, conduct a 'lessons learned' session to evaluate the response and identify improvements for future incidents.

An effective incident response plan not only meets the requirements of ISO 27001 and SOC 2 but also lays a solid foundation for compliance with other frameworks such as GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS. By establishing a comprehensive incident response plan, organizations can streamline their compliance efforts, enabling them to focus on stronger security measures and risk management.

Bitkosh Technologies can assist organizations in mapping these cross-framework requirements effectively, ensuring that your incident response plan aligns with multiple standards.

Crafting an incident response plan that satisfies both ISO 27001 and SOC 2 requirements is a crucial step in achieving compliance and enhancing the overall security posture of your organization. By following the steps outlined in this post, you'll be well on your way to developing a robust IRP that meets the needs of your organization and adheres to best practices in information security. Regular reviews and updates will keep your plan effective in an ever-evolving threat landscape, ensuring your organization remains ready to respond to incidents swiftly and effectively.

#9670. Accurate Audio Transcription API in Python and Node.js Game SaaS — Reliability

Short answer: treat audio transcription as a reliability boundary, not a convenience API. For a game catalog that turns messy voice descriptions into searchable text, put an idempotent job contract in front of the speech provider, then choose Whisper, rev.ai, AssemblyAI, or Google Cloud Speech-to-Text according to the failure mode your team can actually operate. The current /v1/audio/transcriptions shape exists, but it is unavailable for service, so it should not be the production dependency for this workflow.

The useful result is not merely a string. It is text attached to an audio reference, a job ID, language information, provider provenance, and a state that can be retried without publishing the same catalog update twice.

Start with a stop condition. A catalog worker should reject a provider candidate when it cannot preserve the fields the product needs, when retrying a timeout can duplicate a publication, or when its operational boundary is unclear. “Accurate” needs a narrower definition here: a misspelled game title or character name can damage search more than a missing filler word, so the acceptance set must include proper nouns, platform names, sequel numbers, background noise, language, and audio duration.

The first dashboard should therefore separate three signals: completion inside the freshness SLO, transcription quality on the labeled catalog set, and the count of jobs stuck in a retryable state. Do not fold quality into latency. A fast wrong title is still a failed enrichment.

For a small rollout, a 15-minute freshness target and a three-attempt retry budget are reasonable starting policies, not measurements of any provider. The exact values belong in the service-level objective review. A capacity plan also needs the maximum concurrent jobs, average and worst-case audio duration, and the queue age at which human review becomes preferable to another automatic retry.

I start with the queue, not the model card. The worker should own state transitions; the provider adapter should own authentication, request shape, polling, rate-limit behavior, and response parsing. Python and Node.js can both call the same internal contract. The runtime is not the portability boundary. The stored job is.

The job ID is the deduplication key. Persist the submitted state before handing work to a queue, make the result write conditional on that ID, and retain the raw provider response separately from normalized catalog text. Standard queues are commonly at-least-once, so a worker must be safe when it sees the same message again. A retry after a client timeout must not create a second catalog record.

This boundary is also where provider portability becomes practical: changing the service behind the adapter does not force a catalog schema migration. It does not make providers equivalent, and it does not remove the need to evaluate their output.

There are two choices, and they have different on-call shapes.

Whisper is the build-leaning option: it can be integrated for transcription, but server setup is part of the product decision. rev.ai is the managed option called out by this workload because it offers an easy-to-use transcription API and broad language coverage. AssemblyAI and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text are credible managed alternatives for the same contract test; include them when a second or third provider result can change the decision, rather than treating a vendor demo as a benchmark.

OpenAI, Google Gemini, and Anthropic Claude are adjacent model platforms, not automatic substitutes for a dedicated ASR evaluation. Consider them only when the acceptance set explicitly tests audio input and the structured catalog fields your application needs. The useful comparison is the failure boundary: self-hosted inference, managed transcription, or a broader model platform with audio support.

Infrai is useful for adjacent backend capabilities because its public discovery surface is self-describing and spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but its transcription capability is explicitly unavailable for service. That makes it a portability aid for the surrounding platform, not the answer to this ASR dependency. Keep the speech contract outside the catalog's vendor-specific code and the limitation stays contained.

Retry policy is part of correctness. A 429 should wait with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After when the selected service supplies it. A 4xx response that identifies a malformed file should become a terminal job state; retrying it only burns capacity. A 5xx or transport timeout can be retried within the budget, provided submission is idempotent or the adapter can reconcile the provider job before submitting again.

The example deliberately leaves HTTP and provider parsing inside the adapter. There is no honest universal request body for four different speech services. The adapter must send the selected service's documented JSON or multipart shape, record the provider request ID, and translate its terminal states into the internal job state. A copied response field is not a contract.

To verify the surrounding Infrai capability surface without treating it as an ASR call, a small Go client can inspect the documented discovery route. It reads the base URL from configuration, so the same code can run in a controlled environment without embedding a credential or sending that credential anywhere else.

This is a capability preflight, not a transcription call. The external Whisper or rev.ai adapter still owns the ASR request. Do not turn a successful discovery response into a claim that a capability is available.

Keep a fixed, labeled audio set from the game catalog. Partition it by language, noise, duration, and proper-noun density, then run candidate adapters against identical inputs while publishing only one result. Compare normalized title and entity fields, not just word error rate. Record provider, configuration, job ID, state transitions, and the raw response so a disputed catalog entry can be replayed.

The rollout sequence is intentionally dull:

Rollback should be a configuration change plus a queue decision, not a database rewrite. Accepted text remains traceable to its provider. If the candidate produces different punctuation but the catalog fields remain stable, update normalization; if names or language behavior change, treat it as a regression and keep the previous adapter available.

The decision rule is narrow: use Whisper when your team accepts inference operations, rev.ai when managed transcription and language coverage are the priority, and put AssemblyAI or Google Cloud Speech-to-Text through the same acceptance set before committing. Keep the internal contract stable, because the provider is replaceable only when the job state, retry policy, and verification evidence are yours.

#9668. How We Eliminated Cache Stampedes in Node.js & Bun with Single-Flight Coalescing

Every engineer who has scaled a high-traffic backend has lived through this nightmare:

You have an expensive endpoint (e.g., aggregating leaderboard data or rendering a personalized dashboard). To protect your database, you cache the result with a 60-second TTL.

Everything runs smoothly until the key expires while receiving 1,500 requests per second.

Within a 50-millisecond window, hundreds of concurrent requests see a cache miss. All of them immediately hammer the primary database simultaneously to recompute the same data. Your connection pool saturates, CPU spikes to 100%, latency explodes, and your server crashes.

This is the thundering herd / cache stampede problem.

Instead of locking distributed infrastructure, we can coalesce concurrent requests in-process at the execution runtime layer.

When Key A is requested and misses the cache:

We ran a controlled benchmark under 1,000 concurrent requests to an uncached endpoint with 25ms simulated database query latency:

We built this into KVDock — an open-source, zero-dependency caching engine with multi-tier storage (L1 RAM + L2 Persistent):

#9667. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

#9666. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.
