#9654. The Difference Between McDonald's Big Mac & Burger King's Whopper

McDonald's and Burger King need no introduction. Both sit comfortably at the top of the fast-food game, and they have their burgers to thank for their global icon status. Even if you've never set foot inside either chain, chances are you've heard of the Whopper and Big Mac before. They're very different sandwiches, but have spent decades going head to head. The, excuse the pun, beef between the two chains has long been fast food lore. So what better way to settle things than by taking a closer look at what actually sets these heavy hitters apart?

Some differences you'll spot just by looking at the burgers side by side, like the Big Mac's two patties to the Whopper's one, or the extra bun hanging out in the middle of the Big Mac. Others you'll taste. Burger King famously flame-grills its patties, which gives the Whopper a smoky char, while McDonald's cooks the Big Mac patties on a flat griddle for a different, more seared flavor. Then there are the differences that are less obvious, and they have as much to do with history and branding as with what's beneath the buns.

Start with age. McDonald's traces its origins to 1940, well before Burger King's founding in 1954, yet the Whopper is the older burger by a significant margin. Then there's how each chain treats its flagship. Burger King has used the slogan "Home of the Whopper" for decades, so there's no question which burger is its standout. At McDonald's, the answer is less clear. The Big Mac is, of course, nothing short of iconic, dare we say even more so than the Whopper. But that lineup also includes the Quarter Pounder and the cult-favorite Filet-O-Fish, so it has to share the spotlight.

The Big Mac is nearly a whole decade younger than the Whopper. Invented in 1967 by Jim Delligatti, a local franchisee in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, it was first launched nationwide in 1968. The burger was born out of a practical need, with its double patties designed to give steelworkers — frequent customers at Delligatti's restaurant — a more filling meal after completing their shifts.

When it comes to the build, few burgers do things quite like the Big Mac. There are several things that set it apart from the Whopper. It features two beef patties, signature Big Mac sauce (frequently compared to Thousand Island dressing), shredded lettuce, American cheese, pickles, and onions. Already, there are some pretty glaring differences between the two — namely, they share just four ingredients: beef patties, lettuce, pickles, and onions. The Whopper also adds ingredients like tomatoes, ketchup, and mayonnaise. And if we're getting really nitpicky, even the onions are different; the Whopper uses sliced onions while the Big Mac opts for diced.

Obviously, there are two major differences we can't ignore. Firstly, there's the number of patties in each burger. The other is the number of buns. While the Whopper sticks to the standard two-bun setup, with everything wedged in the middle, the Big Mac uses three. The extra piece of bread, known as the club slice, isn't just there for show. Delligatti introduced the middle bun to help give the burger more structure, separating the two beef patties and making the towering stack easier to hold together. It also helps keep the sauce and other toppings from making the bottom bun too soggy under the weight of the fillings, giving the Big Mac its distinctive three-tiered construction.

Arriving a decade earlier than the Big Mac in 1957, the Whopper was created by the chain's co-founder Jim McLamore. It has since become Burger King's signature burger, spawning several variations over the years. These include the veggie-friendly Impossible Whopper, the barbecue-flavored Texas Whopper, and double- and triple-patty versions for those with a bigger appetite. At McDonald's, the Big Mac is something of a Lone Ranger, with no permanent variations on the classic burger offered on the standard U.S. menu.

Beyond their ingredients, another major difference between the Whopper and Big Mac is how the beef patties are cooked. McDonald's cooks its patties on a clamshell griddle before holding them in heated cabinets. Burger King, meanwhile, is famous for its flame-broiling method. Its frozen beef patties travel along a metal conveyor belt through a broiler, where open flames cook the meat. Many have argued that this smoky edge is what puts the Whopper ahead of the Big Mac in terms of taste. Plus, the Whopper claims to contain a quarter pound of beef, which beats out the Big Mac.

Both burgers also have slightly different nutritional profiles. If protein is what you're after, the Whopper has the edge. Despite containing just one beef patty compared with the Big Mac's two, a standard U.S. Whopper contains more beef by weight. That difference is reflected in their respective nutritional figures: A Whopper contains around 34 grams of protein, compared with approximately 25 grams in a Big Mac. This number further pales in comparison to the Triple Whopper, which contains a staggering 78 grams of protein, putting it comfortably in the ranks of the fast food burgers with the most protein.

#9651. Forget The Crock-Pot: 10 Reasons A Dutch Oven Is Better For Slow Cooked Meals

The dutch oven is a beautiful thing. Whether you prefer cast iron, stainless steel, or ceramic, this versatile vessel is one of those essential, timeless pieces of cooking equipment that every home cook should have in the kitchen. And it's a particularly amazing tool for meals that require long, slow cooking — stews, sauces, soups, slow-roasted meats, and so much more — even more amazing than the go-to Crock-Pot.

There's a time and a place for a Crock-Pot, and it can be just the man for the job when you need a time-saving, convenient, and trustworthy cooking method that allows you to "set it and forget it." But the bottom line is that the Crock-Pot comes with its limitations, and it can only accomplish so much... while the dutch oven, which allows for full control and a myriad of techniques while cooking, is far superior for producing delicious, complex dishes.

With several years of experience as a personal chef and decades before that as a home cook, these are the many reasons why I've found that, especially when it comes to a homemade slow-cooked meal, cooking with a dutch oven always wins.

The sheer amount of versatility that comes with a dutch oven makes it a much more valuable player in the kitchen, because you have a plethora of cooking techniques available at your fingertips. Whether you need to sear a piece of meat, sauté your mirepoix, roast a whole chicken, bake an easy casserole, simmer your favorite pasta sauce, or braise short ribs until they fall apart... this single pot can truly do it all.

And even outside of slow cooking, a dutch oven can be used for countless other applications, from boiling water and making tasty mashed potatoes to baking bread and heating apple cider or mulled wine. The possibilities are really endless, which makes this versatile pot a no-brainer whether you're slow cooking or not.

On the other hand, while the Crock-Pot is great at cooking something low and slow, that's pretty much all it can do. It's a singular vessel that cooks food at a low, steady temperature, and most of the brand's traditional slow cooker models offer just three settings: low, high, and warm. These options essentially just alter the overall cooking time necessary for your dish, but the Crock-Pot can't perform any of the other techniques involved in so many classic dishes.

With a dutch oven, you have the opportunity to directly sear your ingredients — and this is everything when it comes to maximizing the deliciousness of your dish. Whether you're cooking a large cut of beef that you're about to slow-roast or a few small chicken thighs that you're going to braise, the ability to get a nice brown sear on your meat in a hot, oiled dutch oven creates that beautiful crispy crust you want when you dig into a piece of meat.

And the same goes for vegetables and other ingredients as well; searing your food first before you slow cook it not only creates better texture at the end, but also gives your dish a head start on flavor. Why? Because searing your food means browning your food, and brown means flavor. It's a crucial step for dishes like a classic beef bourguignon or a beef stew, a comforting pot roast, and a meaty ragu, because it allows you to render any fat, develop more depth of flavor, and add a savory complexity to the overall dish. And that's simply not an option if you're cooking your food in a Crock-Pot.

You may or may not have heard of the term "fond" in the context of cooking, but it's an important part of any flavorful, slow-cooked dish. The fond is a technical French cooking term that essentially refers to all of those browned bits that you scrape off of the bottom of your pan after you cook or caramelize your ingredients. Whether it's drippings from a piece of meat, the browned vegetables that start off your recipe, or even the remnants of a heated tomato paste, those little golden nuggets left behind are loaded with flavor and add dimension to whatever dish you're making... and they wouldn't be possible with a Crock-Pot.

Thanks to the Maillard reaction — a chemical reaction that occurs when the proteins and sugars in your food are heated — whenever you brown an ingredient, it develops new flavors and aromas that transform it into something even more delicious than it was before.

This is especially useful when you're making a sauce, a gravy, or a glaze, because once you add liquid to deglaze your pan, the fond dissolves into that liquid to create the base of whatever dish you're building — providing a savory, flavor-packed element to your dish that takes it to the next level.

Once you plug in that trusty Crock-Pot, you've only got a couple of settings to work with. While you can choose whether your food is cooked low, high, or warm... that's exactly where the Crock-Pot stays for the next however many hours, so each heat level only gets you so far. There's no control over the heat source, and no variability. But a dutch oven gives you both of those things.

You can cook with a dutch oven over the stovetop, which obviously allows you to choose between a high heat, a medium heat, or a simmer. You can also throw the whole pot in the oven, introducing a whole plethora of new temperature options. And you can even use both cooking sources to cook the same dish. You're in complete control of how high the heat is and where it's coming from, which (as long as you're paying attention) will allow you to cook your ingredients more precisely.

Think about something like a beef bourguignon. There are so different elements to this one recipe — searing the meat, deglazing your pan, boiling the alcohol out of the wine, simmering the braising liquid, oven-roasting the ingredients low and slow so the flavors can come together, and reducing the final dish down to that luxurious, gravy-like consistency. You need varying levels of heat to successfully cook this dish, and a dutch oven allows you to cook each and every element to perfection.

One thing you definitely can't do with a Crock-Pot that you can with dutch oven: Reduce. Because you can cook in a dutch oven with the lid off and control the heat, you're able to reduce down whatever you're cooking until it reaches your desired consistency; with a Crock-Pot, you cook at one speed with the lid on, so whatever thickness or viscosity you get in the end, there's no changing it.

What exactly does reduction mean in the culinary sense? It essentially means that you're using heat to evaporate the moisture in your dish. To accomplish this, you cook your ingredients with the lid off or ajar (something you can do with a dutch oven, but not a Crock-Pot), which in turn both further concentrates the flavors of your dish and usually results in a thicker consistency if cooked long enough.

Maybe you're making a tomato sauce from scratch and need to slowly cook the tomatoes down until they become a delicious, concentrated sauce. Maybe you're reducing a pan sauce or a gravy down to that perfect consistency that you can drizzle over your meat. Or maybe you're creating a reduction of red wine or balsamic, transforming it into a rich glaze to elevate your meal. Whatever you're making, being able to reduce while you cook can be a game changer.

Remember the myriad of cooking techniques that you can execute with the dutch oven? Well, more versatility also means that you can cook more complex meals. The option to sauté, caramelize, sear, deglaze, reduce, and more makes the dutch oven a better cooking vessel — especially for multi-step recipes that require more cooking stages — because it allows you to build a dish with more flavor and depth.

With a Crock-Pot, while you can cook some of your ingredients separately before you add them, you pretty much just have one go at it before you slow cook everything (that's the whole point of the "set it and forget it" thing). So the final result, while it can still be delicious for certain applications, is by nature simple and one-dimensional. On the other hand, a dutch oven leaves you with many options and techniques to explore that'll only enhance your final dish.

A great example of this is something like a chili. While you can certainly throw all of your ingredients into a Crock-Pot, slow cook it for hours, and create a perfectly good chili in the end, the different cooking stages that you can accomplish with a dutch oven will make the final dish that much more delicious. You can char your peppers, sear and brown your meat, sauté your vegetables, and reduce everything down to finish it off, which all results in a more complex, flavorful chili.

Dutch ovens, especially those made of cast iron, offer great heat retention. That's because the sturdy, dense cast iron material has high thermal mass, which means it's able to absorb and retain heat and then distribute it slowly and evenly. This stable, consistent temperature makes a dutch oven the ideal vessel for slow cooking and braising.

A Crock-Pot, while it's obviously great at cooking slowly and is still able to cook evenly, is typically made of a ceramic or stoneware insert inside a metal shell; it doesn't actually retain heat well and it relies on continual electricity to keep that heat distributed. But a dutch oven, whether you're using it to slow cook or executing other cooking methods along the way, will respond quickly to heat changes and will evenly distribute varying levels of heat, retaining it even after the heat source has been removed.

Since you have control over the entire cooking process with a dutch oven, you also have complete flexibility as you go. As opposed to a Crock-Pot where you'd typically dump all of your ingredients in at once, when you're slow cooking something with a dutch oven you can choose and adjust the exact order in which you add your ingredients — and that ultimately leads to better texture and better cooking.

Different proteins like beef or chicken obviously cook at a different rate than vegetables do, and even different vegetables have varying cook times depending on the type. More delicate or watery vegetables like zucchini or bell peppers will cook much faster than hearty or starchy ones like onions, potatoes, or squash.

So you may notice that with a Crock-Pot, if you're combining several different types of ingredients (which you usually are), some ingredients will become overcooked or even mushy by the time the dish is done. But with a dutch oven, you can cook down things like onions and carrots first, and then add your softer ingredients later (and adjust the heat accordingly as you go) so that in the end, each and every ingredient has the texture it's intended to.

Having the option to stick your whole entire dutch oven in your oven is huge, because it can make a meaningful difference when it comes to the overall texture and flavor of your meal. While a Crock-Pot is essentially a one-stop shop, a dutch oven is great for something you're cooking low and slow (like a braise), because you can sauté, simmer, and deglaze to your liking to build the initial base of flavor on the stovetop before you transfer everything to the oven to further concentrate and tenderize.

Even if you're not using the oven for the majority of your dish and it's simply a last step to finish things off, having the ability to pop your dish in the oven still goes a long way to elevate the meal. That's because blasting your dish with a higher, circulating oven temperature can provide that final crisp to your edges, give your meat or veggies more of a beautiful brown finish, or melt and meld your cheese together with everything else until your hard-earned dish is bubbling in all its glory.

Last but not least, while the good old fashioned Crock-Pot may be perfectly dependable and convenient... one thing that it is not is pretty. But a dutch oven? It basically comes with built in presentation: You can pull that thing right off the stove or out of the oven and plop it down on some trivets, making it the centerpiece for your kitchen table, and it'll look perfectly presentable.

Presentation may not be everything to everyone, but it's definitely important. Especially if you find yourself hosting others. The dutch oven is the ideal choice when you want to make a meal for a crowd that's somewhat low effort but will still look nice when you serve it. A Crock-Pot just doesn't have the same charm.

The best part is that there are so many colors and styles of dutch ovens available out there that you can really make this piece of equipment your own; it can become more than just a cooking vessel. Whether you go for a Le Creuset or a Lodge, and whether it's a rustic natural cast iron, a classic white enameled coating, or a boldly colored dutch oven that gives your kitchen a pop of personality, you can choose this trusty pot to match your own personal vibe and decor. And your dishes will not only taste great, but they'll also look great inside of it.

The reasoning above is based on years of experience cooking with both Crock-Pots and dutch ovens. As a home cook for decades, a personal chef for several years, and a current employee at a cooking school, I've carefully considered the advantages that a dutch oven has to offer as opposed to a traditional Crock-Pot, specifically when it comes to slow cooked meals.

#9648. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

13. Shanafelt T, Ripp J, Trockel M. Understanding and addressing sources of anxiety among health care professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic. JAMA. 2020;323(21):2133-2134. doi:10.1001/jama.2020.5893

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9645. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

Get more tips for holiday success in our Thanksgiving Baking Guide.

#9644. Only One Chipotle Meat Is Cooked In-Store — And It's Not The Most Expensive Option

Chipotle is our go-to fast casual chain when we want something a little above the usual drive-thru fare, but without the fuss of a sit-down restaurant. One of the main things that sets it apart from traditional fast food is how it handles its ingredients — its stores don't even contain freezers. However, despite Chipotle's pride in its super-fresh ingredients, you might be surprised to learn that chicken is the only meat cooked from raw in its restaurants — and it isn't even the most expensive protein on the menu, clocking in at $11.95 (or $12.55 for its pollo asado) compared to $12.70 for carnitas and $13.95 for both steak and barbacoa (prices may vary).

Chipotle's top-quality chicken appears in everything from tacos and quesadillas to its iconic burritos. Unlike its other proteins, which arrive at restaurants precooked and are reheated or finished on-site, the chicken arrives raw and is later grilled in-store. Before hitting the grill, it's marinated in the chain's signature smoky adobo seasoning, helping give it that distinctive flavor. Chipotle has never publicly explained why only chicken gets this special treatment, but considering it's the chain's best-selling protein, it's hardly surprising that the company goes the extra mile to prepare it fresh.

Fortunately, you don't have to work at Chipotle to get an idea of how its chicken is prepared. Former employees have shared details of the process online, including one Redditor who explained that the chain uses boneless, skinless chicken thighs cooked on a flat-top grill coated with sunflower oil at around 475 to 500 degrees Fahrenheit until they reach a safe internal temperature of 165 degrees.

Interestingly, chicken wasn't always the only protein cooked completely from scratch in Chipotle's restaurants. Die-hard fans will remember that before 2016, the chain also prepared its steak from raw beef on-site, marinating it before cooking it on the grill. However, following a series of highly publicized and controversial food safety outbreaks in 2015, Chipotle introduced major changes to how it prepared its ingredients.

Rather than sending raw beef to its restaurants, Chipotle now uses a sous vide process, in which the steak is vacuum-sealed and cooked at a low temperature for an extended period in a controlled, off-site environment. This method allows the meat to cook evenly while helping control harmful bacteria, allegedly without sacrificing its tenderness. The steak is prepared at a central facility under USDA inspection before being shipped to restaurants, where staff season it and finish it on the grill. However, while Chipotle bosses firmly defended the new process, some customers have complained that the switch was a serious downgrade.

Chipotle's other two meat proteins, barbacoa and carnitas, have long been prepared off-site, in much the same way as each other. Barbacoa is slow-cooked beef, typically from the shoulder, while carnitas is made with pork. Both arrive at restaurants in precooked bags, where they are reheated in-store. According to one Chipotle employee on Reddit, "Carnitas comes in a pre-prepped bag, there's no actual prepping in-store or seasoning from the employees added. We take the bag, shred it up in a pot, cook it until [165 degrees Fahrenheit], then put it on the line."

#9642. For A Smokier Grilled Cheese, Make It South African-Style

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There's truly no going wrong with a grilled cheese. With a crunchy outside and a soft, gooey interior, it's the ultimate comfort snack, even better when dunked into tomato soup – which we have actually been doing for a long time. Beyond being straight-up delicious, it's also budget-friendly, so it's no surprise there are many international variations out there. If you love grilled cheese and smoky flavors, one version you should definitely give a go is the braaibroodjie, a South African classic.

If you've never heard of a braaibroodjie, maybe don't admit that to any South Africans. The sandwich is a cultural staple, and it's a must-have side at any braai, the South African take on a barbecue. It's built from layers of cheese, sliced tomato, onion, and finished with a swipe of sweet, tangy chutney (Mrs. Ball's is the classic choice, which is available online), all tucked between buttered slices of white bread. There's plenty of room for variation without losing what makes it so delicious in the first place, and some less traditional recipes call for extra ingredients like mayo, chili, or even pineapple.

But what really sets a braaibroodjie apart from your standard skillet grilled cheese is how it's cooked. The clue is in the name; the Afrikaans word braai comes from the Dutch word braden (meaning to roast or grill), while broodjie is the diminutive of brood (Dutch for bread). Combined, it roughly translates to "little barbecue bread." In typical barbecue style, instead of a pan, the sandwich is clamped into a hinged grill basket and toasted slowly over glowing coals. That low, steady heat gently toasts the bread and melts the cheese, while the rising smoke from the coals infuses the sandwich with a subtle smokiness a frying pan simply doesn't have the facilities to deliver.

A braaibroodjie is already a pretty perfect sandwich, but that doesn't mean you can't have a little fun with the formula. For a more filling, high-protein braaibroodjie, add shredded chicken, thin slices of steak, or even some canned tuna. If you prefer a deeper balance of sweet and smoky flavors, swap raw onions for slowly caramelized ones to bring out their natural sweetness and add a richer, more savory depth to the sandwich.

The ingredients are the easy part, and the biggest obstacle most home cooks will face when making a braaibroodjie is the cooking itself. The beauty of a grilled cheese is its simplicity, and that doesn't just apply to the ingredients. For many, tending a bed of glowing coals defeats the entire purpose of a low-effort sandwich, and for plenty of us, it isn't even feasible, especially if you're cooking in an apartment with no backyard in sight. If you want to capture the smoky essence of a braaibroodjie without breaking out the matches and charcoal, there are other ways to go about it.

If you want a smoky braaibroodjie that's safe to make indoors, try tweaking your ingredients rather than your cooking method. The easiest place to start is with ingredients that already make up the foundation of the sandwich. Instead of plain old cheddar, swap in smoked cheddar. For an extra-stretchy cheese pull, reach for smoked mozzarella, or smoked scamorza (an Italian stretched-curd cheese, similar to mozzarella but firmer) for an even richer flavor. If you're feeling a little more adventurous, stir some bacon jam into your chutney, or even add a drop or two of liquid smoke — but remember, it's potent, so a little goes a long way.

#9636. Add This Italian-Style Topping To Your Salami Sandwich For A Taste Of New Orleans

If you ever want to expand on a basic salami sandwich, it's never a bad choice to first look to New Orleans, a city famous for its vibrant culinary history. However, the best topping isn't necessarily a roux-rich sauce or some fried shrimp, but olive salad, a rich, tangy, vegetable-forward topping that works perfectly with cured salami.

When people think of New Orleans-style cuisine, they often think first of Cajun and Creole spice mixes, French techniques, and classic staples like the po'boy. But the city has never had a shortage of Italian heritage, which eventually gave rise to olive salad, a vital component of its famous muffuletta. While salami is a common ingredient in this sandwich, a dollop of olive salad alone won't make it one. Still, the unique blend of oil, acid, and salt pairs perfectly with the cured fattiness of salami, delivering an almost creamy texture as you bite through the minced drupes.

While it may seem redundant to pair a tangy meat with a tangy condiment, it's much like adding horseradish to a capsaicin-rich cocktail sauce to create two different types of heat. The ingredients work together to deliver multiple nuances of the same type of flavor, making the taste complex but still quite focused. Pair it with some nice bread to soak up the oil, and you've got a dynamite, three-ingredient meal that tastes like it was made by a true expert.

Creating a truly New Orleans-style olive salad takes a bit of time. While some coarsely chopped canned black olives can add flavor to a salami sandwich, picking the right blend, breaking them down just right, and letting them marinate imparts a greater depth of flavor that makes this topping truly special.

For a more comprehensive range of flavors, use a mix of black and green olives. Kalamatas are always a solid choice thanks to the strength of their flavor, but the large black ones at a salad bar work just fine as well. For your greens, Giada De Laurentiis prefers Castelvetranos, a rich, buttery-soft variety that has next to no bitterness. It's also quite common to add all sorts of pickled vegetables, from carrots and garlic to cauliflower and giardiniera blends, so just about anything veggie- and acid-based will do.

A good olive salad doesn't have the paste-like consistency of tapenade, but it should be soft and tender enough to chew through easily. It's best to chop the ingredients by hand, but you can still use a food processor so long as you stick to quick pulses and avoid smushing everything too much. Letting everything marinate together is vital to bringing out the best in this recipe, so let things sit in your fridge for at least a day. Olive salad can last for weeks in the fridge when properly prepared and stored, so feel free to make a big batch and enjoy it over time.

#9631. 5 Breakfast Sausage Brands That Use High-Quality Ingredients (And 2 To Avoid)

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Breakfast sausage is a great addition to your breakfast by itself, on a biscuit as part of a sausage, egg, and cheese biscuit, or as part of a scramble. But to make sure you're getting the best quality out there, we've created a list of sausage brands that use high-quality ingredients, as well as those you'd probably want to avoid. We looked at how the animals are treated, if they're given growth hormones or excessive antibiotics, and whether the resulting sausage is minimally processed. We also made sure there were no artificial ingredients or excessive fillers.

It might seem like a small thing to look for products with high quality ingredients, but the benefits are many. Chief among them is the positive difference in taste. Breakfast and dinner sausages already taste different, thanks to the addition of sage in the breakfast versions. But high-quality ingredients and meat also taste more savory and often keep you feeling fuller for longer because of the lack of fillers. That can keep the protein high, making the quality sausage a good choice for those watching their macros. So, if you want the best value for your money, alongside the best tasting breakfast sausages, keep this list handy the next time you visit the grocery store.

Applegate Organics has been in business for nearly 40 years, and in that time, the brand has earned a strong reputation as one of the meat industry's most trustworthy companies, thanks to its transparency with customers. The brand's various breakfast sausages are often cited by chefs as a high-quality product because the company takes animal welfare seriously and doesn't use antibiotics on any of the animals it sources.

The pigs used for pork sausage aren't kept in crates, which allows them to be less stressed and gain natural muscle from wandering. They're fed an all vegetarian diet, so there's no animal byproducts in the feed. Applegate's poultry, like turkeys and chickens, are also fed all plant-based diets and given more room to move. This keeps the air quality in the facilities better, which leads to fewer health problems for the animals.

The poultry even get environmental enrichments that allow them to keep their natural perching, scratching, and pecking behaviors, which keeps their stress down and leads to better tasting meat. All of the resulting sausages from the pigs and birds are made without nitrates, preservatives, or artificial ingredients.

Pederson's Natural Farms has been in the pork business since 1992. It only sold three types of bacon when it opened, but the business has greatly expanded since then. The brand now includes beef and bison in addition to a multitude of pork products. All of the meats come from animals that have been raised humanely through sustainable practices, and many of them are certified organic.

This company uses heritage Duroc swine for its breakfast sausages and other pork products. The swine are allowed to roam and fed a vegetarian diet. It has a no antibiotics policy and doesn't use steroids or other growth hormones on the pigs, and the resulting sausages are made without nitrates or nitrites as preservatives. If you're wondering why that matters (because you'll see them mentioned a lot on this list), nitrates and nitrites in processed meats have been linked with high blood pressure and other cardiovascular diseases.

The company doesn't add sugar to them during processing, making the sausages Whole30 Approved, as well as acceptable for those maintaining a keto or paleo lifestyle. The breakfast meat is made with simple ingredients, but no artificial ones are allowed. Pederson's sausages are also certified gluten free, as well as animal welfare certified.

Bob Evans is one of the most recognized names in dinner sides and meat products in supermarkets today. But not everyone is happy with the products Bob Evan's makes, primarily because of a lack of transparency around its practices and potentially problematic preservatives.

The mass-produced brand has no information about animal welfare on its website, unlike the Bob Evans Farmhouse Kitchen, which advertises a commitment to animal welfare and general sustainability. What is known about the breakfast sausages is that preservatives like potassium lactate, BHA, and BHT are used to keep the meat from spoiling. Potassium lactate acts as a way to enhance flavor, hold moisture and keep the product fresh longer, and is generally considered safe to consume.

However, BHA and BHT are a different story. BHA has been under investigation by the European Union since 2018 as a potential endocrine disruptor, which can have concerning effects on animal and human reproductive health. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration began its own inquiry into the preservative in early 2026. BHT is suspected to cause damage to the lungs, kidneys, and liver after repeated exposure, but no formal studies by the FDA are currently underway. Coupled with multiple complaints about animal welfare, Bob Evans is a brand you might want to avoid.

Primal Pastures bills itself as the cleanest meat in America. Started in 2012, this company uses domestically raised and slaughtered pigs that are made into sausage with no fillers. All of its swine are grass fed, with no soy or corn to supplement their feed, and pasture raised, which allows them to be less stressed and attain muscle naturally. All of the brand's meats are also certified humane in Southern California where its processing facility is located.

The pork used in Primal Pasture's breakfast sausages is raised in Nebraska, where they're allowed to roam freely and graze. The farmers rotate the swine from pasture to pasture, ensuring there's always new grass for them to eat. The pigs are never given vaccines or antibiotics, and the sausages are made with no preservatives or artificial ingredients. In fact, the ground pork sausage is made with only six ingredients, while the links are made with seven, including pork, black pepper, sea salt, allspice, sage, celery seed, and a collagen casing.

Jones Dairy Farm might seem like an odd name for a company that primarily sells pork products, but the brand has been selling sausages since the late 1800s. So even though the farm was originally for dairy cows, its claim to fame became high quality pork made from a family recipe. More than a century later, the company is still committed to the welfare of its animals and to using simple ingredients in its products, such as its large variety of breakfast sausages.

This brand makes the breakfast meats in pork, chicken, and turkey. None of the sausages have MSG, fillers, or nitrates included. There's a line of the meats that have no antibiotics ever used on the animals, and none of the sausages contain gluten. The All Natural Pork Sausage Roll has even qualified for the Master Chefs' Institute's Seal of Excellence, thanks in part to its excellent flavor. Jones Dairy Farm breakfast sausages have also earned a spot as one of the items Food Republic taste-testers will always repurchase.

If you frequent the freezer aisles in nearly any grocery store, you'll be familiar with the yellow and red packaging Banquet uses for its Brown 'N Serve breakfast sausages. This budget brand has been around since the 1950s and makes everything from pot pies to frozen dinners to family meals. But it might be most famous for its large selection of breakfast sausages. Unfortunately, many people know the meat for its poor quality, with some calling the brand the worst sausages in the freezer aisle. The brand even took last place on Food Republic's ranking of popular breakfast sausage brands in 2025.

Along with using lower-quality meats, the brand uses BHA and BHT as preservatives. The sausages have a high percentage of soy protein concentrate added as a filler to give the meat more volume and inflate the amount of protein. The meat is also ultra-processed. All in all, this is one to avoid, despite the brand's nostalgic allure.

Niman Ranch might've started as a cattle-based operation in the 1970s, but as soon as the company began partnering with hog farmers in the mid-1990s, the brand never looked back. The company now has a network of over 600 farms and ranches working to raise the best cattle, sheep, and swine in the country. Every animal that Niman Ranch uses for its meat products never has antibiotics or added hormones given to them, and each supplier has to meet strict guidelines for the treatment of the animals and sustainability practices. All of that hard work shows in the taste and quality of the breakfast sausages the company sells.

The breakfast meats are gluten-free and come from pigs that are Certified Humane by the Humane Farm Animal Care program. The swine are fed a 100% vegetarian diet with no animal byproducts, which greatly reduces the chances of the pigs getting sick. The resulting sausage is minimally processed and uncured, so there are no added nitrates or nitrites. You could even try this breakfast meat in this upgraded take on pigs in a blanket.

To find the best and worst breakfast sausages, we combed through the numerous brands that make the product before honing in on how the companies raised and treated the animals. If they were given growth hormones, excessive antibiotics, or low-quality feed, they went on the avoid list. If the animals were treated well and the resulting sausage was minimally processed with no fillers or artificial ingredients, it went on the buy list.

We then narrowed down the buy and avoid lists by looking specifically at customer's reactions to the product's taste and overall value on social media, user review sites, message boards, and professional reviews. The resulting list has what we believe are the best and worst breakfast sausages determined by multiple quality indicators and customer satisfaction.

#9627. What's The Difference Between Yellow And White Chicken Skin?

Between mass-producing farms and local businesses, chicken comes in no small amount of variety. When most people first encounter yellow chicken skin, they can be shocked at the color difference and possibly even think the meat has spoiled. However, this isn't an indication of freshness, but rather the life the chicken had before processing.

Differences in skin color come from a number of factors, and genetics can play a major role. Some lineages are more prone to developing white, yellow, or even black skin. Still, more often than not, the color of chicken skin is due to something called carotenoids, a type of pigment that finds its way into chicken fat. Chickens raised on a processed diet may not get as much of this in their feed, so their skin ends up the familiar, pearly white. Poultry fed through grazing or given kitchen scraps or even corn can pick up enough of this pigment that it tends to dye their fat, much of which is found beneath their skin.

Just like how grass-fed beef tastes different, a chicken with yellow fat can taste quite distinct. If left to graze most of its life, it may taste a bit more complex, with a slight gaminess. In some cases, corn-fed breeds may also develop more fat, making them taste richer. Still, freshness, point of origin, and size are the important factors when selecting the most flavorful chicken at the store.

Whether you're roasting a whole bird or looking to make some crackling, white skin on a chicken is a familiar choice for most people. When prepared properly, it can develop a uniform, golden-brown hue with great flavor and has enough fat and collagen to make a perfectly good stock.

If you're feeding a crowd, it's often best to go with consistency and familiarity to appeal to a broader range of palates. While you may prefer a bit of nuance in your poultry, a white-skinned chicken is often a safe choice. While it may not have quite the complexity of a free-range, grazing bird, it can still have just as much flavor. While not a 100% exact correlation, white-skinned broiler chickens raised in conventional farming operations also tend to be larger than free-range, grazing ones raised at a slower pace on farms equipped to let them have a more varied diet.

While corn can contribute to fat development in everything from cows to chickens, it doesn't necessarily make for the richest poultry available. A plump chicken with white skin may still have had a fairly varied diet, as skin color isn't a reliable indicator of what it ate. Ultimately, the best way to determine a chicken's fat content is to break it down and look for yourself.

From lambs to chickens to humans, beta-carotene is a pigment that can accumulate in fat deposits. More marbled cuts, like dark meat, carry a greater amount of fat and a subtly rich flavor, making them invaluable in certain recipes. If you use skin or fat as a specialty ingredient, yellow-skinned birds can be a great way to add intense meatiness.

Just like lard or tallow, chicken fat is an incredibly potent cooking fat with a respectably high smoke point once clarified. In particular, Jewish communities have a long history of making schmaltz, rendered chicken fat often made from skin and sometimes seasoned with aromatics. Whether you're keeping it on hand in the fridge or adding chicken drippings to Alfredo sauce, it's important to use only a small amount to prevent things from becoming greasy. In this case, you want the most flavorful ingredient possible, and that can start with a yellow-skinned bird raised on a varied diet.

When made right, chicken skin crackling can be better than bacon. While you can always add seasonings to upgrade it, those looking to focus more on the "chicken flavor" of the ingredient may see better results with yellow-skinned birds. Both white- and yellow-skin cracklings are undeniably tasty, but ones made from yellow skin may need only a little sprinkle of salt and a trip to the oven to be truly marvelous. Even if you don't plan on using it right away, any leftover skin from a yellow chicken is always worth saving.

#9623. Clinical Challenge: Cough, Fever, in Person Who Vapes

A 16-year-old adolescent presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of vomiting, tactile fevers, and a mild headache that went away 2 days earlier. The patient denies any abdominal or flank pain, dysuria, diarrhea, or other complaints. When specifically questioned, she acknowledges a slight cough but has no shortness of breath or chest pain.

The patient’s vital signs are normal except for an elevated temperature (100.3 °F) and a pulse rate 133 beats per minute. Initial physical examination is otherwise normal with no rash, tonsillar exudate, rales, murmur, flank tenderness, or other abnormality. Chest radiographs (Figure 1-2) and blood work are ordered. Laboratory results are within normal range except for an elevated white blood cell count (19,000/μL). Pregnancy and COVID-19 PCR tests are negative.

Can you diagnose this condition? What is the most important medical history question to ask?

#9622. Forget Pricey Prime Rib: The Cheaper Cut With Rich, Beefy Flavor

Prime rib is among the most coveted beef cuts. Hailing from the same well-marbled region as ribeye steak, it's a section of meat that's both ultra-flavorful and tender. Typically roasted in a large, multipound intact piece, it's a delicious cut of beef that's slow-cooked, all while retaining a medium-rare interior. Undoubtedly, it's a tasty experience — however, a quality prime rib can cost upward of $20 a pound. Considering 10 pounds is a standard size, the bill adds up quickly.

Thankfully, though, there is a cheaper alternative to consider: a chuck roast. This huge, beefy cut comes from a region directly adjacent to the prime rib, roughly around the animal's shoulder area. In composition, chuck roast offers many similarities to prime rib. While not quite of the same decadent fat density, the cut also contains abundant marbling, as well as a strong beefy flavor. Yet the cost is drastically lower, with chuck roast often available for between $7 and $10 a pound. At around 2 to 4 pounds, it's much more reasonable.

Most often, chuck roast is slow-cooked until well-done, as seen in dishes like beef bourguignon, a favorite of Julia Child's. Yet don't sleep on preparing larger versions of the cut to medium-rare, just like prime rib. Pair a carefully selected chuck cut with the right technique, and the dish offers a similar culinary experience at a fraction of the price.

Not every chuck roast works for a prime rib-like preparation. You'll want to grab a cut with less connective tissue than other parts of the chuck, where it's common. Look specifically for a chuck eye roast, a type of chuck roast that sits right next to the ribeye and thus offers more marbling. In order to recreate the meaty prime rib experience, opt for a larger chuck eye roast — typically around 2 to 3 pounds (larger 5-pound cuts may include tougher surrounding muscles). Especially when topped with a fat cap, such a purchase can help keep the beef moist and flavorful as it cooks.

From here on out, you can cook the chuck eye roast using prime rib-style seasonings, but use a low-temperature cooking method rather than a standard high-heat roast to promote even cooking. You'll want to tie up the beef with twine to promote a uniform shape, as well as add seasonings of choice. Chuck eye roast shines with varied preparation methods, whether a low-temperature reverse sear (low oven or smoker followed by a quick pan-sear) or a temperature-controlled sous vide bath. Cook to medium-rare, rest uncovered for several minutes, then slice. You'll get a mouthwatering prime rib experience at a fraction of the price.

#9619. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

#9616. Scrambled Eggs Won't Be Same When You Grab A Canned Staple With Extra Protein

For a lot of people, scrambled eggs are a go-to when it comes time for a hot, savory breakfast. And why not? They're quick and easy to make, and they've long been considered the gold standard for protein, coming in at roughly 6 to 7 grams apiece.

All that said, though, on their own, scrambled eggs are more of a side, but if you want to make them main meal-worthy, adding one staple ingredient will not only bring more flavor into the mix, but a great deal of extra protein, too. Canned tuna is the game-changer here — it infuses your eggs with a savory umami flavor reminiscent of the sea, as well as a satisfyingly meaty texture.

You could partially scramble your eggs, then add the tuna and continue to cook until the eggs are set, or even mix the tuna and raw, cracked eggs in a bowl and pour both into the pan together. But we highly recommend working in steps, first draining the liquid from the can (don't rinse the fish!) and crisping up the tuna in a hot skillet with some oil, then adding the eggs and cooking until they're set. This gives the tuna a delightful texture boost, and it makes for a much more interesting bite with the contrasting crispy bits of the fish and the softness of the eggs.

Tuna and scrambled eggs are endlessly modifiable, which is great if you take comfort in making the same dishes on repeat, but need a little flavor variation. You might try first switching up the tuna you're using; StarKist's Flavor Fresh Pouch line, for example, has a wide selection of flavors, everything from Honey BBQ to Jalapeño to Thai Chili. Even better, you don't have to drain anything — you can just dump the tuna straight from the pouch into the skillet.

If you're looking to build a little flavor in the oil before you add the tuna, though, you might chop or mince some fresh onion or garlic, respectively. Red onion in particular is an excellent aromatic to use because it imbues the whole dish with a kiss of sweetness that contrasts deliciously with the savory elements. Or you might really lean into the fish factor with a splash of fish sauce and a liquid sweetener, like honey or maple syrup, both to develop deep, savory notes and to allow the sugars to promote super-flavorful caramelization of the tuna.

And then there are toppings. A sprinkle of green onion would add an appealing brightness and bite to this dish, while those looking for outright spice might finish off the tuna and scrambled eggs with a drizzle of hot sauce or sriracha. Or you could shovel the tuna-and-egg combination onto sturdy pieces of toast and top with avocado and plenty of everything bagel seasoning.

#9614. 2 Personality Traits Linked To A Stronger Immune System

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

People with more stable emotions have stronger immune systems, research finds.

People who are emotionally stable usually find it easier to control their urges and are mostly unselfconscious.

Emotional stability is linked to being better at dealing with stress and minor frustrations.

Neuroticism lies at the opposite end of the spectrum from emotional stability.

People who are neurotic typically experience more negative thinking and tend to have worse mental health.

The study included 84 people whose response to a vaccine for hepatitis B was tested.

The results showed that people who were more neurotic — meaning easily stressed, nervous and moody — tended to have weaker immune system responses.

Those who were more emotional stable had a stronger immune response.

Dr Anna L. Marsland,, the study’s first author, said:

“The present findings support a link between trait negative affect and an objective health measure — antibody response to vaccination — raising the possibility that individuals high in trait negative affect or neuroticism may have less protective immune responses.”

In a second part of the study, people were given a stressful task to test their immune function.

The results showed that stress tended to lower people’s immune system response — as previous studies have found.

Along with emotional stability, extraversion has also been linked to a stronger immune system, by a genetic analysis.

Extraverts are typically outgoing, talkative and energetic, meaning they tend to interact with more people.

They are, therefore, exposed to more infections.

A stronger immune response may help to protect extraverts against infectious diseases.

Introverts, meanwhile, tend to have a weaker immune response, as do cautious people.

The study included 121 people who were given personality questionnaires, along with genetic tests and general health screening.

The results showed that extraverts had the highest expression of pro-inflammatory genes.

The effect of these genes is to help fight off infections.

Introverts and cautious conscientious people tended to have a lower inflammatory response.

The study was published in the journal Health Psychology (Marsland et al., 2001).

#9613. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

Cover photo and food styling by Martin Philip.

#9610. Pour Cream Over Diced Potatoes For A Southern-Style Side (Hint: It's Not Gratin)

Cream and potatoes go together better than peanut butter and jelly, and with only a few extra fixings, you can get a seriously Southern-style side dish with very little effort. By just combining potatoes, seasoning, and cream, you get Creole potatoes, a rustic, flavorful recipe with tons of room for experimentation. Enter: Creole cream potatoes.

When it comes to Creole cooking, you'll often find some sort of vegetable gratin on the menu. However, whereas a standard gratin relies on a roux to thicken a cream sauce, this recipe keeps the sauce a bit thinner. Using Creole spice mix instead of Cajun is also quite important, as the higher ratio of herbs pairs perfectly with a bit of cheese, dairy fat, and tubers. While you still want a bit of spice, the parsley, oregano, thyme, and other woody herbs diffuse their flavorful oils into the sauce to then be absorbed by the potatoes.

Since you won't be able to taste this dish as you go, you may want to use a different kind of butter than your usual salted variety. Unsalted ones give you maximum control and, while potatoes do absorb sodium quite well, this is important so that you don't spend an hour baking a dish you later find unpalatable. Most of the baking time for this recipe calls for it to be covered, but don't forget a final few minutes uncovered or even under the broiler to crisp up a last layer of cheese and roast any exposed parts of the potatoes. A little crunch in a swimming rich sauce of cream? Yes, please.

When you're working with such a simple dish, there's always room to add new ingredients or try out new preparation methods. Whether you're picking out different potatoes for a new texture, finding the right balance of fat, or even tossing in some protein, it's hard to go wrong with something this straightforward.

If you like your sauce to be a bit thicker, something that clings to the vegetables, try using russet potatoes. Affordable and available most anywhere, these come loaded with starch but have very little moisture, making them perfect for baking with dairy. This same thing makes them the best variety of spud for scalloped potatoes as they're great at absorbing fat and keeping that flavor on your fork rather than pooling at the bottom of the dish. If you want to keep your sauce thin, aim for a waxier potato, like fingerlings, new potatoes, or any red variety.

Speaking of fat, the one downside of any cream- and butter-based recipe is that it's easy to make it overly greasy. Full-fat cream is vital to getting the right mouthfeel and flavor for the sauce, but you can always use a lower-fat butter or leaner protein as your main. Leaving fat out of other ingredients can also be an opportunity for adding it back through other means. Few things are more Creole than classic potatoes and sausage, but if you want to have less oil, there's no protein more lean and Louisiana than shrimp.

#9608. The Common Vitamin Linked To Weight Loss

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

Higher levels of vitamin D are linked to reduced belly fat, research shows.

The conclusions come from a study including thousands of people.

The researchers measured people’s total body fat and abdominal (belly) fat, along with their vitamin D levels.

The results showed that for both men and women vitamin D deficiency was linked to increased belly fat.

However, for women, low vitamin D levels were linked to both increased belly fat and increased total body fat.

For men, though, low vitamin D levels were linked to more belly fat and more liver fat.

More than half of people around the world may be deficient in vitamin D.

Dr Rachida Rafiq, the study’s first author, said:

“Although we did not measure vitamin D deficiency in our study, the strong relationship between increasing amounts of abdominal fat and lower levels of vitamin D suggests that individuals with larger waistlines are at a greater risk of developing deficiency, and should consider having their vitamin D levels checked.”

It is not yet known if low vitamin D levels are causing more fat to be stored or are a result of it.

“Due to the observational nature of this study, we cannot draw a conclusion on the direction or cause of the association between obesity and vitamin D levels.

However, this strong association may point to a possible role for vitamin D in abdominal fat storage and function.”

Vitamin D deficiency has also been linked to cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune diseases and a higher chance of getting colds.

Foods that are rich in vitamin D include oily fish and eggs, but most people get their vitamin D from the action of sunlight on the skin.

That is why levels are typically lower in the body through the winter months in more Northern climes.

The study was published in the journal Clinical Nutrition (Rafiq et al., 2018).
