#9552. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9548. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9545. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

#9523. ‘These are photos that tell stories about Israeli society’: photography exhibition opens ahead of consequential elections

In Levac’s Bathers in Bental Reservoir in Ramat Hagolan, August 2026, people studiously ignore warning notices Courtesy the artist

“Danger of drowning”, reads one of many warning signs in a recent photograph of a reservoir by the Israeli photographer Alex Levac. “There are maybe ten signs that say not to go into the water, it’s dangerous. And you see tens of people in the water,” Levac says of the contrarian swimmers ignoring the signage and taking the plunge. They all seek respite, come what may.

“These are photos that tell stories about Israeli society,” Levac says. He is known for such photographs, which are at once poignant and bizarre, often capturing within a single frame what might equally pass as an everyday scene or a metaphor. Alongside his incisive views of public spaces, he also takes photographs with a clear political focus. A selection of such images, to which Levac, now in his 80s, has devoted his long and award-winning career, will feature in Black Box, a retrospective opening at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art at a consequential moment for the country: the Israeli legislative elections on 27 October.

The exhibition will open two days before election day and in a satellite location of the main museum campus, the Eyal Ofer Pavilion. It adjoins Habima Square, a central site of weekly protests for the past four years. Taken together, the exhibition’s location, timing and Levac’s subject matter make this retrospective a pointed statement.

“We’re standing before a turning point. There’s a feeling within the public, and certainly I share it too, that something different will happen here,” Levac says. “We’ve been through a very difficult period over the past three years. So maybe in that way, the timing is right. It summarises a certain period, and from here we can start something new.”

Levac’s art-world recognition has come somewhat late due to the photojournalistic nature of his work—this is his first major museum show. “He certainly has a place,” says Sophia Berry, the exhibition’s co-curator and the museum’s associate curator of photography. The Tel Aviv Museum of Art recently acquired more than 50 Levac photographs for its permanent collection, another catalyst for the exhibition.

Most of those acquisitions will be included among the roughly 200 photographs in the exhibition, documenting historical moments, daily life and times of crisis with a characteristic balance of irony, empathy and, occasionally, horror. The show begins with early-career photographs that Levac took after completing his studies in philosophy and psychology, when he was living between England and Brazil, some of which have never been published or exhibited.

The core of the retrospective consists of his prints produced in Israel between 1984 and 2002—charged years that included the first and second intifadas, the Oslo accords, Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination and other important events. Another section will be devoted to his colour photography from 2010 onwards, and a slideshow of his current weekly photographs published in Haaretz, the newspaper where he has been a staff photographer since 1993.

The original negative for one of Levac’s best-known photographs, Kav 300 (1984), will also be on view. Taken during his first year back in Israel after living abroad for 14 years, it documents an incident in April 1984 during which Palestine Liberation Organisation terrorists hijacked a public bus and took 41 passengers hostage. Levac photographed one of the four terrorists being taken into custody, proving that he had been captured alive—and not killed during the rescue operation, as an official report claimed. “Kav 300 changed my relationship to the work. It gave me a shot of adrenalin that lasted many years,” Levac says. “I understood the importance of photography, I saw it with my own eyes.”

Levac has continued his politically focused photography. For almost two decades, he has accompanied the journalist Gideon Levy to take photographs illustrating a weekly Haaretz column, documenting life and hardships in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

“He’s a photographer that is always doing both. It’s part of his great skill: to be on and off duty, all the time,” says Tamara Abramovich, the exhibition’s co-curator and the museum’s photography curator. The polarity of his work—showing the harshest sights, and also the funniest—elicits charged silences and laughter in equal measure.

The past few years have been particularly complex, culminating in this month’s pivotal elections. Levac says he looks for different things now from what he did earlier in his career. “If in my photos before, it was important to me that there be a smile—a certain criticism, but with a wink—now the smile seems redundant, in a way. We’re in a very sad period, very difficult and, in some ways, hopeless,” he says. He recalls one of his early photography instructors claiming that photography can influence the viewer; Levac used to agree. “As time has passed, I’ve changed my mind,” he says. “I don’t think photography can have an impact or make a difference. I think it can expose things and document things, but can it make a change? I doubt it.”

His sentiment reflects the despair of the moment, but it is also at odds with the fact that this 82-year-old photographer still goes everywhere with a camera around his neck. He also requested that his political photographs be the focus of his retrospective.

“Alex doesn’t believe that photography can create change, yet he still continues the work,” Abramovich says. “There’s this tension between the criticism that he has, and his frustration—and a certain optimism.”

#9522. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9520. The Lies We Heard (and Told Ourselves) About ADHD

The world is largely aware of ADHD, but does it truly understand? Jessica McCabe sees lots of room for improvement. Here, the founder of “How to ADHD” reflects on the persistent misconceptions, knowledge gaps, and threats facing people, especially mothers, with ADHD today.

Along the way, McCabe has become a certifiable ADHD spokesperson, a New York Times bestselling book author, and a mother. She has also contributed significantly to the growing de-stigmatization of ADHD and to a still-broiling conversation about how to better recognize and support women with ADHD.

“The more we talk about it, the more shame dissipates,” McCabe said during her recent ADDitude webinar, “The Lies We Were Told About ADHD: An ADHD Awareness Month Conversation.”

When McCabe posted her video, there was no YouTube #ADHD channel and TikTok did not yet exist. Today, social media is bursting with research, analysis, and validation. It’s also wrong more than it is right.

According to a 2025 study, more than half of the claims made in the Top 100 TikTok videos on ADHD were false. Almost 90% of videos were created by non-experts, and only about 20% of ADHD content was deemed clinically useful by trained professionals.1

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

“The [videos] that are validating and make you go ‘Yeah, that’s me,’ are not necessarily the ones that are accurate,” McCabe said.

She cited a claim circulating on social media that individuals with ADHD lack object permanence, as an example. Object permanence is the understanding that objects, people, and places continue to exist even when they cannot be seen. People with ADHD experience inattention and executive function challenges such as poor working memory, which may contribute to forgetfulness, but that is distinct from poor object permanence.

McCabe recommended checking sources on any health information found on social media. “Google Scholar it,” she said.

From a young age, people with ADHD hear that the frequency and intensity of their emotions are a problem. They’re told they are “too much,” and that their feelings overwhelm and distract others. McCabe says she grew up suppressing her emotions in hopes of combating that narrative. Now, she is working to actively “unlearn” that negative perception of her feelings, and she hopes others can do the same.

“Some of us have forgotten it’s okay to feel. It’s okay to have emotions when you have ADHD,” she said. “The emotions are not actually the problem. What you do with those emotions might be problematic, but by trying not to feel things, that actually creates other issues.”

Acknowledging and creating space for your emotions keeps them from exploding and/or festering — neither of which is healthy.

Executive dysfunction carries a lot of shame and guilt for people with ADHD. Society generally doesn’t recognize that challenges with working memory, organization, and prioritization, for example, are part and parcel of ADHD. Criticism is a constant, and many people add to the pressure by berating themselves with negative thoughts.

“When you don’t have an explanation, you accept the ones that are handed to you by society,” McCabe said. “It looked like I was flaky. It looked like I was uncommitted. It looked like I didn’t actually care about things.”

Executive functioning often fluctuates. Sometimes you can complete a task; other times, that same task feels impossible. In those moments, you may beat yourself up by saying, “I should be able to do this. Why can’t I do this?”

As McCabe shared, sleep quality, personal interest, support systems, and other factors influence a person’s ability to manage ADHD challenges in the moment. Not all of those factors are obvious, or within your control.

“A lot of those things are invisible, so unless you pick it apart and look at it, you don’t know why you’re struggling. You’re just like ‘I shouldn’t be,’” McCabe said. “Anytime I’m like ‘I should be able to do this,’ [I ask] what’s the evidence for that? Have you ever in your life been able to do this without help consistently? No? Then you shouldn’t.”

The effect of childbirth on the ADHD brain is largely unknown due to a critical research gap. What we do know is that women with ADHD are six times more likely to experience postpartum anxiety and five times more likely to experience postpartum depression than their neurotypical peers.

McCabe, who welcomed her daughter in 2024, suffered from postpartum depression. The supports she relied on during pregnancy stopped working and postpartum hormonal changes brought her to a very dark place mentally and emotionally. She was admitted to a partial hospitalization program for postpartum depression, where she received treatment while caring for her child.

As critical research slowly takes shape, McCabe believes strongly in normalizing this experience for mothers and entire families by talking openly about it.

“I think [the outcome] would’ve been different if I didn’t understand this wasn’t my fault that I was struggling,” she said. “Because the idea of what a mom is supposed to look like and what I looked like were so different that I could have piled so much shame on myself. And I think that shame would have made it so much worse. I wouldn’t have reached out for help. I wouldn’t have wanted to tell anybody I was having these thoughts or struggling with these things.”

“For so long we’ve been asking, ‘How do we get people with ADHD functional?’” she said. “Now I think we can ask a new question: How do we get them happy? How do we make it so they can live a good life? What does a good life with ADHD look like?”

Maybe the objective shouldn’t be to never struggle with focus, time management, memory, or emotional regulation ever again, but to use the tools you’ve developed to build a life that looks good and feels comfortable to you.

“Success and happiness to me with my ADHD is like having this powerful stallion that I know how to take care of, ride, accomplish incredible things, have excitement and adventures, handle the rough and challenging moments, while not getting bucked off, trampled, or left behind in the dust,” Katherine, an ADDitude reader, commented during the live event. “It’s still now working to unlearn all of the suppressive things taught through school that wanted to teach me to break the spirit of the stallion, whip it into submission, and then lock it in the stable and feel ashamed of it and what it needs instead of learning how to work and thrive with it.”

#9519. Philadelphia Museum of Art receives $20m to establish new education centre

Students from Philadelphia take a tour of the Asian galleries at the Philadelphia Museum of Art Photo: Mark Stehle, courtesy Philadelphia Museum of Art

The Philadelphia Museum of Art (PMA) has received a $20m gift from the Philadelphia-based philanthropists Lois G. and Julian A. Brodsky. The money will be used to establish an education centre that aims to strengthen the museum’s engagement with the region’s students, children and families.

The design for the forthcoming Lois G. and Julian A. Brodsky Learning and Engagement Center will be unveiled next year by the Philadelphia-based architecture firm MGA Partners, which spearheaded the redesign of the museum’s 4,000-sq.-ft auditorium in 2017. The Brodsky Center will occupy the PMA’s north wing and span around 19,000 sq. ft, featuring multi-purpose spaces and art studios.

“One of the main considerations guiding the design process is to transform the north wing of the museum into a dedicated, dynamic education hub that expands the museum’s capacity for creative learning and civic engagement,” Daniel Weiss, the museum’s director, tells The Art Newspaper. “It will be an intentional, purpose-built space that ignites limitless educational experiences grounded in the PMA’s extraordinary collection.”

The museum currently offers free admission for those aged 18 and under. It welcomes around 36,000 students each year from both Philadelphia schools and those of neighbouring cities and states. The Brodsky Center will focus on building connections between younger visitors and their families—particularly people from underserved communities—with the museum’s encyclopedic holdings, spanning approximately 245,000 works of art.

“We hope the centre breaks down barriers and builds relationships through the open-design approach, and that it will provide space to gather, host students, hold community-driven dialogue, develop teen and multi-generational programmes, and nurture partnerships that strengthen Philadelphia’s cultural life,” Weiss says. “One of the ways we will measure reach is by listening to our visitors to determine who we are missing, who is not coming and where we need to extend our invitation so that we have every neighbourhood represented.”

The Brodsky Center is the first major capital project since the PMA’s $233m renovation and expansion, designed by Frank Gehry and completed in 2021. The project reimagined around 90,000 sq. ft of the museum and added 20,000 sq. ft of galleries and public spaces.

The Brodskys each have decades-long relationships with the PMA. Lois joined as a volunteer in 1982, was a weekday guide from 1986 to 2019 and currently serves on the committee for conservation, European art, prints, drawings and photographs. Julian—a co-founder of the telecommunications conglomerate Comcast Corporation—joined the PMA board in 1995, became a trustee emeritus in 2024 and currently serves as the vice chair of the museum’s library and archives committee.

The couple have made other significant contributions to the PMA, including funding exhibitions and installations—such as the reinstallation of the 19th-century European painting galleries in 2019. In 2009, they participated in a matching campaign to establish permanent endowments for curatorial and other museum staff. The Brodskys also contributed substantially to the museum’s 125th-anniversary campaign, which raised $250m in 2005 and saw the Constantin Brancusi gallery renamed the Lois Green Brodsky Gallery.

#9517. Mapping the ADHD Brain: How Neurotransmitters and Medication Work

The unique structures, wiring, and functionality of neurodivergent brains, according to science.

Why do one person’s ADHD symptoms differ from another’s? The answer lurks inside the structural and chemical differences of the ADHD brain.

No single brain region is the source of ADHD. However, subtle variations in brain structure, function, connectivity, and neurochemistry shape the neural networks that govern attention, motivation, reward, emotion, and self-control.

The regions involved in ADHD traits include:

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

The brain comprises billions of nerve cells called neurons. These neurons work in circuits, passing signals to each other that allow our bodies to think, move, remember, manage emotions, and control impulses.

Between neurons is a tiny gap called a synapse. To get messages across, neurons release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters into the gap. The neurotransmitters cross the gap and attach to receptors on the next neuron to help the message continue. Afterward, the brain clears neurotransmitters away in a process called reuptake.

The neurotransmitters dopamine (DE) and norepinephrine (NE) help the PFC hold goals and instructions in mind, filter distractions, and guide behavior. They also help reward circuits decide what feels interesting, urgent, or worth doing.

In ADHD, these signals don’t support those circuits and processes as strongly or consistently as they should. Task-relevant information may fade too quickly, while distractions, impulses, emotions or immediate rewards may pull more strongly. This is why ADHD is sometimes described as a “signal-to-noise” problem: the useful signal is there, but it may be drowned out by competing noise.

ADHD is linked to differences in how brain networks communicate and coordinate attention, motivation, emotion, and self-regulation.

ADHD medication can optimize brain signals by slowing the reuptake of DE or NE, increasing their release, or activating receptors that strengthen signaling. All of this helps guide attention, motivation, and self-control.

COMPARING THE IMPACTS OF ADHD MEDICATIONS

New insights: Functional connectivity data show that stimulants enhance performance by increasing vigilance and perceived task value.11 In other words, stimulants help the ADHD brain stay motivated and engaged with non-preferred tasks.

In addition to dopamine and norepinephrine, a third critical neurotransmitter is serotonin, which helps to regulate mood and emotion, both deeply relevant to the ADHD experience.

Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, and many people with the condition also live with mood disorders. Almost half of adults with ADHD are also prescribed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) – medications that increase serotonin levels to regulate mood, emotion, and sleep.

Viloxazine, a non-stimulant, became the first ADHD medication in the U.S. to also modulate serotonin. Beyond targeting ADHD symptoms, the medication was shown to improve co-occurring depression and anxiety in adults with all three conditions.12

Centanafadine (Simtriyo), a stimulant ADHD medication recently approved for children aged 6 years and older and adults, is a norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin reuptake inhibitor (NDSRI). Trials show that the medication improves symptoms in both groups and in adults with ADHD and co-occurring anxiety.13

Untreated ADHD impacts neural connectivity.14 Unstable brain connections increase risk for the development of anxiety, depression, insomnia, emotional frustration, and other challenges. ADHD medication enhances neural connectivity, but there are other ways to promote neural growth, protect the brain, and decrease risk for secondary issues.

Greg W. Mattingly, M.D., is an associate clinical professor at Washington University School of Medicine.

#9516. Musée du Louvre, Musée d’Orsay and other Paris institutions to close on Saturday due to protests

Students from the École du Louvre blocked access to Musée du Louvre on 19 October to express their suppor" for the high school students' movement and to denounce "police repression"

Following scenes of looting and vandalism in several French cities, from Lyon to Limoges , on the sidelines of last weekend’s protests over the cost of living and in support of high school students, there is considerable apprehension on the eve of new demonstrations planned for this Saturday, 24 October. Curfews and bans on demonstrations are multiplying throughout France. In Paris, a march, the route of which has been approved by the police prefecture, will depart from the Place de la Bastille and proceed to the Place de la Nation. The government, overwhelmed by the violence of 17 October and heavily criticised since, has announced a reinforced security deployment.

In this highly tense context, shopkeepers are not the only ones to “close their doors”, or even barricade themselves in. Following the announcement of the early closure of the 2026 edition of the Art Basel Paris fair at the Grand Palais starting this Friday evening, several museums will remain closed this Saturday during the protests, for fear of further unrest.

The ministry of culture has announced the exceptional closure, as a security measure, of the Musée du Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Orangerie, and the Picasso National Museum in Paris. In coordination with the Paris Police Prefecture, the ministry “has asked all institutions under its supervision to implement all necessary measures to ensure the safety of visitors, the protection of staff, and the preservation of artworks,” according to a press release.

On the Paris Musées side, the Carnavalet Museum, the Maison de Victor Hugo, the Cognacq-Jay Museum and the Petit Palais will be closed.

The Louis Vuitton Foundation, currently exhibiting the Gustave Fayet collection, has also announced its precautionary closure, as have the Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection and the Cartier Foundation (all weekend). Many Parisian galleries will do the same this Saturday, including Poggi, Christian Berst – Art Brut, Magnin-A , Gagosian, and Hauser & Wirth.

Museums and cultural venues in the region are also taking precautions. It is advisable to check before visiting.

#9515. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9514. 3 Ways to Extinguish Emotional Reactivity

Smoldering flames may reignite. Rather than burying your emotions, try these strategies to minimize and outsmart them.

It starts with a spark — a critical comment, a goal unrealized — and our emotions quickly catch fire. This blaze can be public and palpable, or private and hidden. Spiraling thoughts, avoidance, self-criticism, and other reactive patterns may create a temporary sense of control, but they backfire over time, trapping us in reactivity loops that increase rather than reduce distress. They can also paralyze us.

When distressing emotions threaten to consume you, try the strategies below to neutralize or dampen them.

Observation, or mindful attention, is a foundational skill for emotional regulation because it creates a pause between stimulus and response.

To build this skill, alternate between focusing on your breath and on how your emotions live in your body – rapid heartbeat, knots in your stomach, tight fists, etc. Then expand your focus: What sights and sounds near and far do you notice? Now bring your attention back to your breath.

Fight the impulse to stuff down your emotions, as unpleasant or distressing as they may feel. For helpful cues, try saying “allow” aloud or picturing a green light through which your emotions can pass.

[Read: 7 Truths About ADHD and Intense Emotions]

Try these visual exercises to buy yourself even more time to process emotions. Imagine…

[Read: Why We Feel So Much — and Ways to Overcome It]

Shifting how you view a situation can modify your emotional response to it. Keep these reframing statements somewhere close and read them in moments of distress:

Over time, these skills will help you gain emotional clarity and choose actions that align with your values, not your reactive urges. In practice, that might mean taking a risk despite anxiety, putting the phone down instead of sending an angry text, forcing yourself to take a walk instead of isolating, or delaying gratification.

Douglas Mennin, Ph.D., is a professor of clinical psychology at Teachers College, Columbia University, in New York City.

#9512. Chicken with Cajun Cream Sauce

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – SO cozy! I love this meal!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 17, 2026

That tomatoey, creamy, shallot-infused gravy is something I haven’t been able to stop thinking about.

I made this dinner for my family on the first barely chilly day a few weeks ago. I think my body had just been waiting for permission to go fall cooking mode, and I just unleashed.

Pan-fried chicken. Luscious, savory Cajun cream sauce. Homemade mashed potatoes. Green beans. Apple crisp for dessert.

I served it in deep bowls and we let the girls eat on the living room floor, using the coffee table as their table, while we watched American Ninja Warrior together with the windows open – which, frankly, is the move of two parents who are feeling extra generous and a little out of their mind with the joys of early fall weather. But that meal will be a top 5 meal for me this year, for sure. We all devoured in silence and then cozied up with full bellies to watch some ridiculous TV together.

Here’s an idea I keep coming back to: shrimp. Like what if you just made the sauce, and then threw a pound of uncooked jumbo shrimp in there? It would poach right in the sauce! I haven’t been able to pull myself away from the chicken and mashed potatoes combination, but I feel shrimp should at least be considered.

Hope this recipe gives you all same cozy fall feelings it gave me.

Also a big fan of using the air fryer here, if you’re not feeling the pan-frying.

This picture shows the shallots minced; I also really love to do this with a thinly sliced shallot, sliced on a mandoline. The shape will give you these little ribbons through the sauce.

Add cream and broth, and simmer till it’s GLORIOUS.

I mean, showstopper material right there.

My favorite combo for serving is mashed potatoes and green beans. LIGHTS OUT. So good.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – loving this easy, cozy weeknight dinner!

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

#9511. Study: Narcolepsy Medication Found to Improve Adult ADHD Symptoms

The orexin 2 receptor agonist called ALKS 7290 parallels stimulants’ path as a narcolepsy medication that evolved into an ADHD treatment.

An investigational narcolepsy medication called ALKS 7290, an orexin 2 receptor (OX2R) agonist, offers a new therapeutic approach for ADHD, according to results from a recent Phase 1B proof-of-concept study. ALKS 7290 is the first OX2R agonist to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms in adults with the condition, according to the drug’s manufacturer Alkermes plc.1

“OX2R agonists will represent an entirely new class of ADHD treatment, breaking the traditional barrier between stimulants and non-stimulant treatment,” says Greg Mattingly, M.D., a consultant on the Phase 1 and upcoming Phase 2 trials.

Stimulants remain a first-line treatment for ADHD in adults. However, not all patients tolerate the side effects of or see benefits from stimulant medications. According to an ADDitude survey of more than 11,000 adults with ADHD, 78% of respondents taking amphetamines and 70% of those taking methylphenidate experienced some side effects, compared to 66% of adults taking non-stimulant medications.

The drug works by selectively binding to and activating orexin type 2 receptors, proteins in the brain that regulate alertness, arousal, and appetite. This targeted approach could minimize potential side effects and drug misuse, according to Mattingly.

“Unlike traditional stimulants, orexin 2 receptor agonists have no direct effect on dopamine reuptake or release,” says Mattingly, Associate Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the Washington University School of Medicine. “Orexin 2 receptor agonists modulate pathways in the brain that are associated with vigilance, reward, and alertness while decreasing impulsivity. By minimizing direct effects on dopamine reuptake or release, they are considered to have a lower abuse potential.”

The two-week double-blind, parallel-group trial included 50 adults with ADHD and 88 adults without. Participants with ADHD were randomly assigned to receive ALKS 7290 at a total daily dose of 20 mg or 50 mg in split doses or placebo.

As early as day six, patients taking ALKS 7290 demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms, as measured by the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS), and in overall ADHD severity, as measured on the Clinical Global Impression-Severity Scale (CGI-S).

By day 14, treatment with ALKS 7290 reduced median baseline AISRS total scores by 14 points for the 20 mg dose and 19 points for the 50 mg dose. Median CGI-S scores declined by one point with the 20-mg dose and two points with the 50-mg dose.

ALKS 7290 was generally well tolerated at both doses, with mild side effects including insomnia, dizziness, change in sustained attention, and constipation.

The ORX2 agonist also shows promise in treating narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), a common co-occurring condition with ADHD. (Approximately 25% of people with narcolepsy have ADHD.).2 In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Orzeyful (oveporexton), a first-in-class OX2R agonist tablet indicated to treat narcolepsy type l (NT1) in adults.3 Takeda Pharmaceuticals, Orzeyful’s manufacturer, expects the drug to be available in November 2026, pending DEA scheduling.

NT1 is a chronic sleep disorder, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy, and sleep disruptions, resulting from a deficiency in orexin-producing neurons.4

ADHD and narcolepsy share several overlapping symptoms related to arousal and wakefulness. Before becoming standard ADHD treatment, stimulants like amphetamine and methylphenidate were used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness found in narcolepsy patients.5

“Our longest surveillance of the safety of amphetamine comes from following people with narcolepsy for their entire lives,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. Today, Ritalin (methylphenidate) and Adderall (amphetamine) are both central nervous system stimulant medications approved for the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy in adults and children.

While it is too soon to know if the OX2R agonist used to treat narcolepsy will likewise evolve into a standard ADHD treatment, the parallels to stimulant medications are clear.

“What’s exciting for clinicians was the fact that ALKS 7290 had dose-related improvement in ADHD symptoms with dramatic improvement seen early and sustained throughout the two-week study,” says Mattingly, founding partner of St. Charles Psychiatric Associates. “While preliminary, the level of improvement obtained with this molecule after two weeks was similar to what is typically seen after four to six weeks in a trial of methylphenidate or amphetamine molecules for ADHD treatment.”

Results from a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of ALKS 7290 in adults with ADHD are expected in 2027.

1 Alkermes Announces Positive Phase 1b Results Demonstrating Clinical Proof-of-Concept for ALKS 7290 in Adults With Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Press Release. September 21, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://investor.alkermes.com/news-releases/news-release-details/alkermes-announces-positive-phase-1b-results-demonstrating

2 Ren, Jiafeng, Zhao, Xianchao, Su, Changjun, et. al. (2024). ADHD in narcolepsy: A closer look at prevalence and ties. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2023.105471

3 FDA Approves First Drug to Treat the Full Range of Narcolepsy Type 1 Symptoms. Press Release. August 5, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms

4 Krahn, L.E., Zee, P.C., Thorpy, M.J. (2022) Current understanding of narcolepsy 1 and its comorbidities: what clinicians need to know now. Adv Ther. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-021-01992-4

5 Konofal, Eric. (2024). From past to future: 50 years of pharmacological interventions to treat narcolepsy. Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pbb.2024.173804

#9510. As riots scar Paris’s luxury storefronts, Maison Guerlain opens art exhibition on Champs Elysées

Installation view of L’Heure des Possibles at Maison Guerlain in Paris

On Tuesday 20 October in Paris, among all the luxury boutiques on the avenue Champs-Elysées bearing the scars and graffiti sprayed on shopfronts by rioters just days before, Maison Guerlain opened L’Heure des Possibles, an exhibition of works by 33 artists.

The pieces, four of which were specially commissioned and the rest loaned, were sourced in response to one of Guerlain’s signature perfumes, L’Heure Bleue, and the period of twilight the fragrance takes its name from.

Wall-based works by well-known names including James Turrell, Annette Messager, Christian Boltanski and Ugo Rondinone have been installed throughout the historic maison alongside up-and-coming contemporary artists such as Marie Bovo, Xie Lei and Valentin Fougeray.

First founded in 1828 by Pierre-François-Pascal Guerlain, the Guerlain family built their hôtel particulier on the site in 1914.

“We need a moment of blue after all the black,” says Guerlain’s director of art, culture and heritage, Ann-Carolin Prazan, regarding the demonstrations that protested the state of education and cost-of-living in France, and which have been overshadowed by violent outbreaks by some ultra far-left groups. A VIP evening event marking the opening of the exhibition on 20 October at Maison Guerlain was cancelled.

“Paris is the capital of culture,” Prazan adds. “People want to support artists and culture; we must not be felled. I think we have to say ‘enough!’ now.”

Installation view of L’Heure des Possibles at Maison Guerlain in Paris

Despite President Emmanuel Macron saying “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days, France is bracing for another round of rioting this weekend, with Art Basel in Paris announcing yesterday that it is closing two days early as a safety precaution (Guerlain is a host partner of Art Basel Paris). Steps have already been taken to remove and protect some of the public sculptures that are dotted around the French capital as part of the Art Basel public programme.

Maison Guerlain, however, will remain open all weekend, according to a spokesman.

The perfume designer has an almost 200-year history of collaborating with artists from Matisse to Yves Klein and Lee Ufan. Its famous Bee Bottle, created in 1853 as a wedding present to Empress Eugenie de Montijo with Napoléon III, has been reinvented by contemporary and street artists including JonOne, Wassim Mraihi and Géraldine Gonzalez.

The company now has a vast archive of 25,000 works in its warehouse, many of them perfume bottle designs.

For the past 20 years, Guerlain has also held contemporary art exhibitions in the flagship boutique—a programme that has supported contemporary artists. The Paris-based artist Alexandra Mocanu, who has collaborated on an intricately embroidered work with the Swiss creative studio Retinaa, says Guerlain’s support has been “crucial” while she looks for a gallery in the French capital.

Prazan says she was unsure when she first started installing Modern and contemporary art in the maison in 2006. “It’s hardly a white cube,” she points out. “But it works.”

Unlike other luxury brands, Guerlain has remained streamlined in the products it makes, sticking to fragrances, skin care and makeup. This is perhaps unsurprising, given that the company was bought out in 1994 by LVMH, the world’s largest luxury goods conglomerate which manages more than 75 brands and made more than €80.8bn in revenue in 2025. Bernard Arnault, who owns LVMH, is one of France’s biggest art collectors, though the Guerlain collection remains a distinct entity.

The focus is now on the 200th anniversary of Guerlain in 2028, when a global exhibition featuring 20 artists is due to take place in Korea, Dubai, the US, China and Japan, among other places. “It’s going to be big, and it’s going to be totally unique,” Prazan says.

For its 30th anniversary, the Musée d’art moderne et contemporain invited the artist to show his monumental sculpture The Big Wave as part of a major retrospective

#9509. 36 Healthy Fall Dinners With All The Cozy

Healthy and nourishing fall dinners that are super cozy, too! Some of my favorite bowls, salads, soups, and more!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 18, 2026

Fall dinners are here, and honestly, this is the kind of food I wait for all year. Steamy bowls, creamy sauces, roasted veggies, cozy spices, and meals that make the whole house smell amazing. These healthy fall recipes bring all the sweater-weather comfort while still being nourishing enough for an everyday weeknight!

To call out a few of my all-time favorites from this list:

Nourishing food should still feel generous, cozy, and completely delicious, and these dinners are it!

Roasted sweet potatoes topped with creamy chipotle sauce, spicy ground chicken, avocado, cilantro, and pickled onion. My family loves them!

I love this Kale Apple Salad! Kale, brussels sprouts, rosemary cashews, apples, fried bread cheese, crispy shallots, and crisp apple maple dressing!

Silky carrot soup topped with spiced ground beef and toasty pine nuts! Bright, savory, warming, all the best things!

Amazingly creamy, saucy chickpea curry served over rice with a dollop of chili crisp and a side of cucumber salad. Ready in 20 minutes!

One of my family’s favorite easy dinners that works SO well for meal prep! Sweet potatoes and ground beef get dolloped with a creamy high protein street corn style dip that is bonkers delicious.

Detox Crockpot Lentil Soup – a clean and simple soup made with onions, garlic, carrots, olive oil, squash, and LENTILS! Super healthy and easy to make.

The BEST Grain Bowl! Roasted root vegetables, earthy grains, dried fruit, dark leafy greens, buttery goat cheese, and lusciously creamy balsamic dressing.

Coconut Curry Salmon! Broiled salmon with a salty-sweet spice rub, creamy coconut curry sauce, and steamy rice to soak it all up.

These tempeh bowls are a true fall favorite! Massaged kale, sweet potatoes, roasty marinated maple-mustard tempeh, crunchy apple, and an unexpected pile of briney sauerkraut.

Lemongrass, ginger, shallot, and the brightness of lime! These broth bowls have got it all – luscious broth, fluffy rice, protein, and fresh herbs.

Saucy shredded chicken, yellow rice, pickled onions, greens, and cilantro pesto on top. It’s a flavor and color delight!

We are living our best bowl life this week. Seasoned sweet potato wedges and chicken meatballs or rotisserie chicken all piled onto a plate with a little puddle of punchy green avocado mojo sauce. Yes, wow, repeat.

This 7-Layer Beet Salad is a stunner! Studded with cooked beets, supremed oranges, chopped pistachios, creamy truffle ricotta, and a bit of fresh mint. So fresh, so good!

These House Favorite Brussels Sprouts are the best side veg and are speckled with bright bursts of cranberries and nutty walnuts. The perfect addition to any meal!

These Spicy Peanut Tofu Bowls are a meal prep / weeknight dinner life-saver! Crispy tofu, roasted veggies, fluffy rice, and a spicy sweet peanut sauce all over top.

These beauties need to be on your table! Deeply roasted rainbow carrots, swizzles of tangy garlicky yogurt sauce, a golden drizzle of honey, and festive pistachio crunches on top.

Healing Chicken and Rice Soup that is limey, salty, and so fresh! Garlic-ginger-infused broth, shredded chicken thighs, tender jasmine rice, fresh herbs, and peanuts. YUM.

Brussels & Kale Caesar! Papery-thin shreds of brussels sprouts and chopped lacinato kale, tossed with a creamy, garlicky, avocado-based vegan caesar dressing, topped off with the most addicting cheezy garlic croutons.

Autumn Glow Salad with Lemon Dressing – a MUST for healthy, glowy eating! Roasted cauliflower, sweet potato, grains, and apples.

Healthy and versatile bowls that come together under a generous drizzle of addictingly creamy vegan chipotle tahini sauce.

A savory coconut creamy broth, swirls of chili oil floating on top, beautiful veg and cubes of flavor-soaked tofu, and a pile of steamy rice at your service.

A cozy, hearty, humble bowl of this Country Chicken Stew is waiting for you! Chicken, thick-cut bacon, navy beans, veggies, and fresh herbs all simmering in one big pot. It’s a good one, friends!

This Hot Honey Salmon is giving off major fancy-to-eat-but-not-fancy-to-make vibes. Spicy-sweet salmon coated in fresh garlic, stone ground mustard, sweet honey, and flecks of red peppers flakes. It’s a magical little number!

Harissa Chickpeas with Whipped Feta! Perfectly spicy/saucy/tomato-y chickpeas smothered in creamy, garlicky whipped feta and served with naan, lemons, and cucumbers. Your next weeknight wonder!

Easy Veggie Enchiladas! Saucy, cheese, filling, cozy, and packed with any roasted veggies you want. Super versatile and easy to make!

Guess what’s for dinner? Creamy, spicy, delicious red curry lentils, made in the Instant Pot.

Amazing Mushroom Bowls with Kale Pesto! Smoky, sweet, salt mushrooms (or tempeh!), caramelized pineapple, peppers, and dollop of kale pesto, all served over rice.

Sesame Beef and Broccoli! Full of protein, green broccoli goodness, and sticky-sweet garlic and ginger flavor. Perfect at-home takeout!

Creamy Thai Sweet Potato Curry – packed with nutrition! Our favorite easy, healthy, winter comfort food recipe.

These Roasted Cauliflower Hummus Bowls are LIFE-CHANGING. A bed of garlicky creamy hummus, piled high with spiced roasted cauliflower, and a speckling of fresh lemony tomatoes and herbs.

Spicy Shrimp with Cauliflower Mash and Garlic Kale – tender-sweet shrimp and smoky garlic kale over creamy cauliflower mash. The most DELICIOUS fake-fancy weeknight dinner!

Roasted Vegetable Bowls! Crispy tender roasted veggies, buttery avocado, all together in a bowl with a drizzle of green tahini sauce.

15 Minute Meal Prep Cilantro Lime Chicken and Lentils! The BEST easy protein powerhouse meal prep. Just 15 mins of prep and totally hands-off cooking!

Instant Pot Sweet Potato Tortilla Soup! A smoky, limey, tomato-rich broth with onion, garlic, jalapeño, crispy tortilla strips, and tender chunks of sweet potato.

These healthy chipotle sweet potato skins are stuffed with a chipotle-sweet potato filling, black beans, corn, and topped with cheese. SO GOOD.

Healing Bowls: turmeric sweet potatoes, brown rice, red quinoa, arugula, poached egg, lemon dressing.

Fall is for snacking, too! Here are some of my favorite healthy snacks – for myself, or for my kids’ lunchboxes!

#9508. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#9506. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

This soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

First kiddo went down with a GI bug last night, so I figured it was the perfect time to try this recipe! I used homemade bone broth to make the soup and added a Parmesan rind while it simmered. It’s salty, brothy, and gently flavored. We’ll see how my sick one tolerates it, but my other two kids thought it was cozy and delicious. The star pasta is a fun texture.

This is simple and delicious. I’ve made it twice now. This past time, I put the broth (sans vegetables) through a fine mesh strainer which helped get a nice and smooth texture.

Also, grocery stores near me sell relatively small carrots. I used a one-pound bag of carrots and found that to be an appropriate amount.

My son and husband woke up not feeling great this morning and I was running to Walmart anyway, so I decided to pick up the few things I needed to make a batch of this soup today!

Sadly, they didn’t have the pastina pasta, so I used bowtie pasta. I also used chicken bone broth instead of the Bouillon. And I also cooked boneless skinless chicken thighs in with the broth and veggies for some extra protein.

This was so simple and so delicious. I have a ton to freeze and a ton in the fridge for my boys to eat throughout the week as they work on feeling better.

Simply amazing! So much flavor from such simple ingredients. I’m sensitive to garlic and onions so I kept them whole to add flavor to the broth and then discarded them before blending the veggies and the soup still had so much flavor!

Is there any downside to using an immersion blender instead of taking it out and using a regular blender? Thanks!

I’ve been rocking a cold for the last 1 to 2 weeks but with pregnancy, you don’t get to take anything helpful; finally got a chance to try this, and this hot silky broth is so so good. I gave it a verrrry generous amount of fresh cracked pepper along with the grated Parmesan.

So glad you enjoyed it, and hope you feel better soon!

Very good! I had to saute longer. The only thing is when I blended, I still got a crunch from the celery.

Of course I should have checked here first! DUH! I am 100% going to blend the veggies in next time – what a great idea!

Delicious as written! Who knew these simple ingredients could make such great soup? It reads to me like a gourmet soup starter at a fancy restaurant….

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

I couldn’t wait to try this soup. It truly did not disappoint. I used orzo because that was the smallest pasta that I had in the pantry. Will be keeping a container in my fridge for quick & healthy lunches. Thank you for the recipe.

This soup + your miracle no-knead bread is my entire personality all fall/winter long!!

Okay, now it’s ours too. Thanks for the rec!

I have made pastina before with broth bu I sure do love the extra step of blended veggies! Brillant. I will make this recipie from now on.

I’m not sick, but I couldn’t wait to make this. I had everything except celery, so I substituted a bunch of parsley (which I removed before blending) and half of a green pepper. It’s easy and so delicious and comforting, and I usually have these ingredients at home, so it will be in the regular rotation.

Thanks for making the recipe, and appreciate your notes!

LOVE Italian penicillin soup! It is a staple in our house for flu season!!

I add bell peppers into the veggies and feel like it gives an extra depth of flavor. We also do the Parmesan rind trick. I’ve always used an immersion blender and haven’t had an issue with the texture.

I don’t think I can wait for someone to get sick!

Hahaha right? Good for sick days AND regular days.

OMG, this reminds me of something my mom would make for me as a child when I was sick. Except hers used condensed cream of celery soup lol. Thanks for bringing the spirit of that dish into the 21st century so that I can share it with my son. 🙂

Cream of celery! So interesting, I’ve never heard of that in a soup like this! Love uncovering those food memories. 🙂

Hi, do you know if I can cook the Stelline directly in the broth? Looking forward to trying this recipe! Thank you!

Okay technically yes, I think you could! But here’s why I prefer not to:

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

– the experience of pouring the broth over the noodles is really fun. 🙂

Could you use an immersion mixer and keep the veggies in the bowl? Or will that change the outcome? Thank you!

I do think you could! I decided not to because I wanted it to get really silky smooth broth which I felt like my Vitamix could do better. But if you aren’t concerned about a perfectly silky smooth texture then I think it would absolutely work and it would save you the transfer!

Any thoughts about using a bone broth / regular broth blend?

Was wondering the exact same thing! My guess is it won’t get quite as smooth?

Do you really use 10 cups of broth? Does look like that much in the pictures.

Yes, 10 cups! Happens almost every time I make this that I start with 8 cups, thinking it will be enough, and then I always end up adding 2 more (at least) for a total of 10 cups to get the level of brothiness I’m looking for!

Some of it will depend on the thickness of your carrots and celery, so if you aren’t sure you could always start with 8 cups and then add to get your desired final consistency.

Throw a parm rind in while it’s simmering and thank me later. 😊

YES! I don’t always have a parm rind sitting around so didn’t include it in the list, but ABSOLUTELY SO GOOD for the flavor. (and would just have to remember to pull it out before blending!)
